review_text:
Finally, a ramen noodle shop on Clinton.  But to call Ivan's a ramen shop is doing it a huge injustice.  Neglectful, even.  The diversity of the menu offers up such things as fried tofu (more on this later), daikin radish salad, pork meatballs, thousand year old deviled eggs, and deep fried chicken livers.  Yes, I tried all of those in addition to a huge bowl of ramen.  All on the first day of my "it's almost too late to get ready for the beach" diet.  Oh well.  

After many trials and tribulations with ConEd getting this quaint and well laid out shop open, Michael and Jenn have shown what they can do and damn, it is good.  The backyard is absolutely gorgeous with the beautiful mosaic full of discovery and whimsy.  The décor is simple and classic and exemplifies Ivan's approach to providing new interpretations on classic dishes without going overboard.  
On top of all the deliciousness, the Coney Island Tofu was the most awesome presentation / twists I have seen in a very long time.  Fried tofu, covered in a miso and mushroom chili and a splash of yellow mustard.  At first, I didn't get the reference but yes, they really do look like chili cheese fries but none of the heaviness and heart-clogging regret.

I had the triple garlic / triple pork tankatsu.  This is a no brainer.  Figure it out and then order it.

The spicy red chilli ramen has a wonderful heat that sneaks up on you without being overpowering.  It is about the flavor, not the heat but it all comes together in a mouth-watering concoction of broth, noodles, and all sorts of goodness.

I have to also bring up the dirty rice.  I don't know the name on the menu but it is an amazing aray of spices and monk fish liver.  Now usually, fried rice is pretty ok at best but what the guys in the kitchen do with this is downright, well, dirty.  I loved the texture and depth of the caramelized rice and the slow heat build-up as I plowed through the dish that I really should have been sharing but too bad, I'm the grown up.

Well done, guys and welcome to the neighborhood.   Now go do that voodoo that you do, SO WELL!
I was just there for Friends and family, (disclaimer, I am friends or family with some of the staff there), it was so good. It has a very innovated and fun menu.

Had the distinct pleasure of trying out Ivan's Ramen. I was looking forward to great things as I'm a huge fan of the slurp shop and I was not disappointed.

One of my biggest qualms about ramen shops is that appetizers and small dishes are often an afterthought and haphazardly thrown together. Here, they receive every bit as much effort as the ramen and I must say it shows. The fried pork meatballs had a surprisingly melty, hot center. The anchovy salad made great use of Japanese mayo, the shrimp had a nice balance of sweetness and spice, and the pork masubi was an absolute star (we got two orders). 

The triple garlic mazeman was outstanding and had a taste I have yet to find outside of Ivan's world. The spicy chili pork ramen took spiciness to whole new level (be aware that this is not your typical mildly spicy broth). 

Overall a creative and delicious experience, will come back again, especially to sit outside when it gets a bit warmer.

After whetting our appetites with the excellent ramen at the Slurp Shop in Gotham West Market, Ivan Ramen has finally opened his long-awaited full restaurant, and it was well worth the wait and the repeated delays.

As expected, there was a decent-sized line when I walked up at 5:30 (opening time) on opening day. Unexpectedly though, the line moved very quickly, and they were extremely efficient and professional the entire night. They were already running it like pros on just the first night.

It's seems like a small restaurant, but they actually have quite a large seating capacity, with some tables up front, followed by some bar seating in the middle area against the wall and facing the kitchen, and then many larger tables in the open garden in the back near that cool pig mural. Ivan himself was walking around the entire night, cool as a cucumber, just chilling and chatting up the customers.

We were seated and ordered a good selection of the menu by 5:45, after which our food started to come out pretty quickly. We got a sampling of items from the "Crisp", "Hot" and "Ramen" sections of the menu (completely neglecting the "Cold" section, which was probably a bad idea since it was quite a heavy meal):

- Roast Pork Musubi ($6)
This was a delicious start to the meal. Two little bite-size pieces, these were not like traditional musubi, but were instead kind of like unwrapped versions. A delicious hunk of pulled pork and tomato topping a little ball of rice, all placed on top of a crispy piece of seaweed. I took it in one bite and it was excellent.

- Ankimo Dirty Rice ($14)
This was one of the best bites of the night - it was a good portion of fried rice with tons of monkfish liver, which I never previously realized was so delicious. The rice was piping hot and slightly crispy and had some decent kick to it, which had me reaching for my water continuously. This is a great choice if you like some spiciness, or just some really good fried rice.

- Pork Meatballs ($9 for 5)
Listed under the "Crisp" section, these meatballs were amazing. They indeed had a light, crispy exterior, and a really soft, creamy interior. There was apparently tofu mixed in with the pork, which would explain that great texture. These are a must for a really satisfying starter.

- Tofu Coney Island ($11)
One of the dishes I read about frequently leading up to the opening, this can be described as a rendition of "vegetarian chili cheese fries". Instead of fries, there is lightly fried strips of tofu. Instead of chili, there is miso mushroom sauce. Instead of cheese, there is yellow mustard. Add some onions to the mix, and this makes for a very interesting dish that somehow works for the most part. It almost tasted like you really are eating chili cheese fries for a second, especially at first when the tofu is still really hot and crispy. Some of the tofu pieces were cut a little thicker though, and the larger pieces of mushiness were a little off-putting. Overall though, this is definitely worth a try as it quite different.

- Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen ($15) Fully Loaded (+ $5)
This was incredible. Really rich and porky from the 1) tonkotsu broth, 2) chashu pork and 3) crispy bacon bits (there's the triple), the flavors are so strong. The chewy, springy whole wheat noodles were even better than I remembered from the excellent bowls at Slurp Shop. The "Fully Loaded" option is a must to get that perfect egg, as well as the tasty roasted tomato (and chashu pork, which already is included in this bowl). This is heavy, but well worth getting filled up on.

- Four Cheese Mazemen ($15)
Another pretty much brothless bowl, this was also extremely rich and overwhelming. His take on mac & cheese, it reminded me more of a ramen version of carbonara. The broth was so thick, coating each delicious whole wheat noodle with so much of that cheesiness. This was even heavier than the triple pork bowl, but it's another must try.

Ivan Ramen just makes really good quality food. Everything here was very well made and delicious. It all came out nice and hot, and service was perfect throughout, particularly impressive given it was opening night. I will definitely be back to try the rest of the menu, and hopefully once they have some dessert available. I especially need to try that Okonomiyaki with scrapple and the Spicy Red Chili Ramen. Maybe the salad or broccoli next time too, so I live long enough to try it a third time.

Ever since the Slurp Shop opened up in Gotham West Market I'd been making the trek to the far western reaches of Hell's Kitchen just for a bowl of ramen. Now that the full restaurant is open on Clinton I only have to walk a few blocks to satisfy my ramen cravings!

The menu is a bit expanded here with a nice variety of small plates for sharing. Definitely get the pork musubi. I split an order with a friend and one wasn't enough, we had to order seconds!  

Wait time for 2 around 9:30 on a Friday night was about 30 minutes but they'll take your number and send a text when your table is on deck.

I take ramen very seriously.  Ivan's ramen is as good as any I've ever had.  Wonderful, warm team takes great care of you and Ivan is just such a nice guy.  This will be a weekly spot for me, no doubt.  Thanks for a great meal and a terrific night.

I must have come at the right time. I had planned to join the masses on line right before the dinnertime opening of 5:30 (my whole life feels like a long line) however the nice weather prompted me to linger a bit longer than usual at a nearby park. However, the promise of ramen was too strong and I made my way in the springtime heat trying not to idle as I passed a bunch of my favorite restaurants along clinton street. I got here right around 6 and the two of us were seated immediately even though the restaurant seemed very full. I took note of the open backyard which I plan to request next time to dine al fresco. It definitely looks more like a lunch place with all the counter seating though. It definitely looks like a place I could order a shake and some fries. I am hoping the chef adds dessert to his menu.

I was glad that we were seated towards the front of the restaurant next to a family having a mothers day ramen meal. We sat fortuitously along a wall mural filled with brightly colored characters from my childhood like the snap, crackle and pop elves from the rice crispy commercials, tony the tigerrrr and the chubby little frog from honey smacks. The service was very smiley and we got our food in a timely manner and they constantly kept checking on us which was nice. Also nice to see chef ivan making the rounds and chatting with the customers. It would have been nicer to see him making his magic in the kitchen though.

We ordered a glass of yuzu lemonade to share since it was an 80 degree day. The lemonade was very light and sweet and not very tart. It tasted more like a clementine or tangerine juice with a hint of lemon. 

We opted to try two types of noodles after we both fought over who would get to order the triple garlic mazemen. In the end we also ordered the tokyo shio ramen. The triple pork triple garlic mazemen was such a palate pleaser with its garlic and pork enriched sweet tonkotsu sauce and a helping of the whole wheat noodles were topped with scallion, brined roasted nickel thin garlic slivers, two pieces of rich fatty pork belly chashu, crispy bacon crumbles and a small sprinkle of garlic powder. Less broth and good noodles make it definitely slurpable for the bib inclined like me. I wish I had 2 orders of this or maybe an extra noodle portion since this was really good. You could order it fully loaded with a soft boiled egg, roasted tomatoes and extra chashu for an extra fee. As it was I did get hungry just a few hours later. I cannot live on ramen alone. The tokyo shio ramen was a dark chicken broth flavored with dashi and sea salt which came with the big piece of chashu pork and a serving of rye noodle topped with a small mountain of scallions. I was less pleased with this dish because the scallions really overwhelmed the broth and other elements of the bowl and I had to stop drinking it because it left an oniony flavor in my mouth which I tried to wash out with my yuzu lemonade. Less scallion and maybe bean sprouts or bamboo would have contributed nicely to this dish for texture. I do wish there was more than one piece of pork though. At first I thought it was two pieces but it was just one larger piece but the pork itself was very tender and did not leave a fatty taste. The rye noodle was softer than I anticipated but was satisfactory. These whole wheat and rye noodles were an interesting change from my udon and soba diet. Didn't taste like I was having healthy noodles at all. My favorite is still the triple garlic mazemen.

I will be back to try everything in the crisp appetizers menu such as the tofu coney island, the pork meatballs, the ebi shrimp and the jfc chicken livers but there are tons of appetizers to choose from besides these like thousand year old deviled eggs and roast pork musubi. As well as some of the other interesting noodles like the four cheese mazemen and the spicy chili ramen and I definitely hope to come back to dine outdoors on the back patio.

Chef Ivan thanks for opening a nice little noodle stand in the LES I hope to make this another one of my usual spots.

After reading on grub street that it was opening night on Friday, I headed over to the LES to try my luck as a 1-top.  I am glad I did.  The ramen is excellent and the restaurant is sure to be a hit (probably a big hit which will result in terribly long lines).  

First off, the staff is already very well trained and professional.  They use an ipad to figure out seating arrangements and will call you when your table or seat is ready.  The place is a bit bright, but well decorated.  My only knock on the decor is that the space is quite narrow up front, although they seemed to have garden seating in the back?  

As for the food, it was great.  I had the 1000 Year Old Deviled Egg, which was tasty and a nice starter.  I then got both the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen and the Tokyo Shio Ramen.  That is too much food for 1 person, but I wanted to taste both and then bring the rest home for my lady, who wasn't feeling well.  

The mazeman was very rich in flavor and the noodles were excellent.  Pound for pound though, I would say that Yuji Ramen in the Bowery Whole Foods has more flavorful and exciting mazeman.  That said, it was still delicious. 

As for the ramen, it was on par with Ippudo and the other greats in the city.  I do not think is significantly better than ippudo or totto though. It is well seasoned and has a nice depth of flavor.  

Finally, the sake is expensive for how much you get if you pay by the glass. 

tl;dr:  great ramen, though not transcendent.  Nice space, but will probably crowded and overrun for some time, if not permanently.

Very surprised that there was no wait around 8pm on a Tuesday, given this place just opened a week ago and I would have thought that there would be a line. Lucky us I guess. So we got a table in the back for 3, ordered the deviled eggs which was my favorite of the night. We also shared the waffle okonomiyaki, and that was ok. Now for the ramen... it was just ok. I've been to the slurp shop and was not impressed, again I was not very impressed here. I had the Shio Ramen, and nothing stood out. Maybe it was from all the anticipation of how amazing it will be, ended up not blowing my mind.

I visited Ivan Ramen on an overcast, misty night, the perfect kind of night to indulge in a hot bowl of ramen.  I'd been excited about the opening of this location, what with all the hype and press, so I was surprised to find that the wait wasn't that long (25 minutes or so for 3 people on a Wednesday...granted, we did sit at the bar).  My two friends and I decided to go all out, as we'd heard great things about not only the ramen, but the appetizers as well.  We began with a nigori sake, which was cold and cloudy, a nice change from the standard clear sake served warm.  

We started with two orders of the deviled eggs, two orders of the roast pork musubi, and one plate of pork meatballs.  Everything was delicious, but the roast pork musubi was the biggest hit.  The roast pork, juicy roast tomato, and wasabi went perfectly with the nori wrap.  The deviled eggs had a depth of flavor I wasn't expecting, and the pork meatballs were great, but I'd probably order something else in their place next time.  It was all a very interesting marriage of flavors and a welcome reinterpretation of existing dishes.

I had the spicy red chili ramen.  I liked the addition of minced pork over chashu.  I must admit, however, that it was almosttttt too spicy for me.  It's very upsetting to actually say that because I'm the kind of person who puts hot sauce on literally everything and now I can barely eat a meal without it.  I'd vote for a touch less spicy and a little more broth flavor.  My friend got the 4 cheese mazemen, which was delicious, even for someone like me who can take or leave cheese.  Next time I'll probably get the shio ramen and add spice.

This sums up my experience: at one point near the end of the meal, hot and thirsty from all the spice and wanting more water, I got the server's attention and blurted out, "Could I please have some more ramen?"  Freudian slip.  Did I want more ramen?  Obviously.  Could I have fit anything else in my stomach?  Definitely not.

Was asked to go have ramen here, I was excited but didn't know what to expect. 

Fast forward to the food. 
I don't know what the hype is about. Ramen is garbage here. Too salty, no flavor, and they charge for extra broth. Also if you want extra noodles it's not standard, they must ask the chef. Absolutely BS. 

This place is also not cheap. For their prices I much rather wait longer and go elsewhere. Honestly I have had better ramen at random sushi places and even at an airport. 
Nothing was good here except for the service. 

Let's be real, if their first shop isn't getting good reviews, what makes you think this place will be any better. Avoid at all cost.

Came here on opening night around 7pm. There was no wait for a table for 3, we sat in the cute outdoor area in the back.

We were all starving so we ordered a bunch of apps and ramen to share. We got:
Pork Meatballs: 4 meatballs, fried on the outside but still tender and juicy on the inside.
Braised Ox Tongue: a hefty portion of ox tongue over beef broth with a smear of hot mustard on the side. The tongue was so tender, I loved it! 
Ankimo Dirty Rice: monkfish liver, lemon sofrito, scallion. The rice has a nice kick to it, my favorite dish of the night
Roast Pork Musubi: 2 pieces of pork with roasted tomato over seaweed. I ate the entire thing in a bite and all I tasted was salt, salt and more salt. PASS
Lancaster Okonomiyaki: scrapple waffle, charred cabbage, pickled apple, maple kewpie. The "waffle" was very disappointing. It didn't have any crisp a normal waffle should have. 

We ordered two mazemen fully loaded which comes with egg, pork chashu, roasted tomato. Mazemen does not come with any broth. 
Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen
Four Cheese Mazemen: I am a huge cheese lover so this was the dish I was looking forward to the most. It fell short, tasted like Kraft's instant mac & cheese mixed with a lot of salt. 

Everything came out to $45/person. Overall I was not impressed with the hype that surrounded this place. I appreciated that the manager actually came to our table at the end and asked how our meal was. I was honest and told him everything was over salted. He apologized and said he would talk to the cooks about measurement and consistency. I'll cut them some slack since it was opening day. Maybe I'll come back to try the other ramen dishes in the future.

A pleasant surprise!  The shio ramen's surprisingly complex amalgam of animal essence flavors with the firm chewy noodle texture makes this a sure-fire addition to the ramen-craze.  The garlic mazemen ramen as a dry version created a flavor explosion with a yummy mix of garlic, pork bits, and I-don't-care-what-else it was so good!  :). The other stars of the night were the hot roast pork musubi (with tomato, roast pork, and seaweed magic) and the lemonade drink.  There were definitely some interesting items that I wanted to try but I can only eat so much.  Can't wait to come back.

I've been waiting for this place to open since I live less than 10 minutes away. 
My friends and I came here grand opening night for dinner and the place wasn't as packed as I thought it'd be. I guess I missed that sign.

We sat outdoors under an awning since that was an option.

We ordered: 

Braised ox tongue - the mustard in this really killed it for me

Pork Meatballs - I've had better meatballs

Ankimo Dirty Rice - not bad, wished there was more flavor

Roast Pork Musubi - salty! 

Lancaster Okonomiyaki: nothing special

Triple pork mazemen - charsiu was pretty good, and the noodles were decent. 

Four cheese - very salty!


The waiters were too attentive, but missed many of the essential details. We were asked several times how everything was by each waiter, and we constantly had to ask for utensils, plates, and glasses of water.

I have been stalking the opening of the NYC Ivan Ramen since I first tried Ivan's Smorgasburg pop-up in November, 2012. The flavorful broth and toasted rye noodle had me hooked and wanting more. We stopped by around 6:45pm on a Sunday night, and there was no wait. Things were starting to pick up later in the evening though. There are enough tables in the restaurant that you can get near the place, and the staff has been properly trained.
 
The interior is cheerful with nods to both Tokyo and NYC. One prime example: the Japanese movie poster of Woody Allen's "Manhattan" casually hanging on the back of the bathroom door. They have tables, counters, and rear patio.
 
But on to the food! We decided to split a side of Chinese broccoli with garlic to start. This dish was served cool, not warm, and the thinly sliced garlic was incredible. They packed a lot of flavor into those chips. The leaves of the broccoli were better than the stems, as they soaked up most of the sauce. I wished there were more broccoli leaves than stems; it's harder to get a broccoli stem as flavorful.
 
There are a couple of different types of ramen to choose from, but my cheesy bias led me to the 4-cheese mazemen. I wasn't sure how this was going to turn out. At best it could be like carbonara or mac and cheese, but at worst it could be heavy and gummy - a real gut-bomb. Fortunately, it was the former. Mazemen naturally has less broth, and this was a good thing. The cheesy broth did not weigh the dish down, but instead added to the al dente noodles (around the same thickness as spaghetti), toasted panko crunch, and tangy spring onions. The last component was pickled bean sprouts, which were the best surprise of all. Their vinegary acidity was so great against the richness of the cheese. I was sooo happy this dish was not too heavy, and I savored every bite.
Beautiful Resturant, delicious/unique food, incredible customer service. My experience here was 10/10. Loved it - highly recommended!

My friend and I started off with the thousand year old deviled egg, and though expensive, it was full of so many great flavors that I'm surprised that another reviewer called it unmemorable. The Okonomiyaki with scrapple-- SO. FREAKING. GOOD.

And the Spicy Red Chili Ramen was recommended to me by the nicest server I've ever had, I think his name was Elio. It was tasty, but so spicy that I could barely finish it. Normally I'm not a wimp when it comes to spice, but maybe mine was overly spiced. The pork was also a bit "meh" in my opinion. I've had better.

My foodie friend had the Tokyo Shio Ramen and he was really pleased with it. I'd say the service was what makes this place shine, but I'll definitely be back to try to rest of the menu.

It's their opening week so I expected their customer service to be good which it was. I was pleasantly surprised by the knowledgable waiter. He was very detailed even with our questions on the food. Also the atmosphere was wonderful. Very modern with a nice outdoor patio area with awning so if it rains, you are covered. Also they were very nice about not rushing folks even though there is a line outside. 

The reason I'm giving it three stars is because the ramen was just sooo salty. I had the triple pork/triple garlic ramen, and I had to order extra broth so that I could tone down the sodium. I don't know about most people but I get ramen partly for the broth. My friend had the spicy ramen and the noodles in that one was delicious.  I really enjoyed the appetizers too. They were delicious and I will be back for those! We got the beef tongue, pork with pickled plum tomato, 1000 year old deviled egg, and the scrapple okinamiyaki. A friend of mine has the veggie ramen and stated the same thing that it was too salty and needed more veggie mushroom flavor or something.

Astonishingly original dishes, great service, and a vibrancy both in atmosphere as well as the food's actual preparation make Ivan Orkin's new spot a definite hit. I was pretty blown away tonight.

Ok, so first we went with 2 orders of Roast Pork Musubi which my brother and I downed before we could take a picture or even speak. They were excellent. If you have had the pork donburi at the Slurp Shop these kind of tasted like more refined bite-size versions of that.

Next was Lancaster Okonomiyaki, which was great with an amazingly delicate, almost nutty tasting scrapple waffle (which was definitely more wheat than pig-based) topped by these bright cubes of pickled apple.

We also had the Ankimo Dirty Rice which was actually the most decadent and heavy of all the courses. The monkfish liver and fried bits of garlic gave the dish an exceptionally rich feel. 

Finally, we got the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen and the Four Cheese Mazemen. I actually want to say which one I enjoyed more but I am afraid I just can't. The cheese one is actually really tangy (which I was not expecting) and which saved the dish from being too heavy. It really was like a carbonara exploded with umami. The Triple Pork Triple Garlic is actually a really restrained, principled dish, and the hearty, thick wheat noodles are especially complemented by the rich broth. 

Just be aware Mazemen is not ramen. It does not contain as much broth and is more of a noodle dish than a soup. Some reviews below complain about the broth amounts so, if you are looking for a bowl of ramen with a solid amount of broth, go with one of the four ramen dishes you will find just below the two mazemen. 

Anyway, Ivan has crushed it. I will be back so, so many times.

Excellent & Novel Fare

After several interesting appetizers -- they even managed to refactor Caesar Salad -- I had rye noodles in rich broth, augmented with pork, egg, et al.  Very well executed and delicious.  Do not miss the Yuzu Lemonade.  Exceptionally warm and attentive staff.  Looking forward to returning.

So I never made it too Gotham West. way. too. damn. far.

Lucky for me, this place opened up. Went yesterday on a rainy day and was seated immediately at the counter. The place is larger than it looks - there's a decent amount of seats in the restaurant and the covered area in the back.

We started off with the pickled daikon, which I highly recommend. Delightfully tangy with a slight hint of spiciness. I would pass on the Lancaster Okonomiyaki. It came out lukewarm and the mayo and sauces way overpowered the scrapple.

Onto the noodles. I had the triple pork and triple garlic mazeman, which was delicious, though salty. I like the chewiness of the wheat noodles. Friend's shoyu ramen was okay. The rye noodles are rather thin. I would say the portions are a bit on the smaller size.

Decent drink menu, nice service. I wish they offered more toppings than just egg/more meat/tomatoes.

Best Bites: Pickled Daikon XO, Ponzu Honey Mustard, Ox Tongue + Broth + Mustard, Roasted Tomato in Broth, Red Chili Ramen Broth

MAY 25, 2014 - The menu is divided into three sections before ramen: cold, crisp and warm. If you're hungry, what you should do is order a total of 2-3 items before your ramen (we went overboard intentionally).

We received a very strong recommendation to start with pickled daikon xo, so we went with it and were rewarded in-kind. A mild pickle on the daikon made each strand a great canvas for the crispy, spicy xo sauce (dried shrimp and scallop chili oil), and it took great restraint not to order a second plate after our first bites.

Also from the cold section came the little gem salad with baby anchovy and parmesan crisps and a tofu garlic dressing. Big pluses in this dish included the dead-on texture of crisp, supple lettuce leaves and the lightness imparted by tofu in the dressing. My personal preference would to have been hit with more anchovy flavor as I think it would have elevated what was otherwise a tasty dish.

Next up, we jumped into the crisp section for some Japanese fried chicken or JFC, breaded chicken hearts and liver with a killer ponzu mustard dipping sauce. I love the concept and think it succeeded thanks to a star sauce and the unique cuts featured in the dish. While the double-dredging was a good call to stand up to the liver flavor, the heart was over-dredged for me. I love the texture of heart, but it's not all that gamy and got masked in the process.

We then got sidetracked in the warm section...for a while. First to the table was the Lancaster okonomiyaki, a scrapple waffle with charred cabbage, pickled apple and maple Japanese mayo. No doubt one of the most unique dishes in the city, but perhaps lacking in a strong enough savory component to balance the toppings. Not sure why the waffle didn't quite do the trick, but I expected it to be meatier for some reason (admittedly, scrapple isn't pure meat so that explains a lot).

We also ordered the dirty rice with monkfish liver, lemon sofrito and plenty of scallions, intending to take it home with us rather than scarfing it down at the table. I quite enjoyed it, despite not really having any standout flavor to cling to; it's just a really solid fried rice dish.

We didn't actually order the braised ox tongue with beef broth and spicy mustard. We'd been sitting on the patio during a downpour under the awning and getting a bit wet in the process, so the very kind wait staff offered us some tongue for our troubles (=P). We obliged, again out of gluttonous curiosity, and loved it. That mustard packs a helluva punch, but in the right quantity with a great broth and tender strip of beef, it's absolutely delicious.

By this point we were satiated physically, but mentally still questing for ramen. I ordered the Tokyo Shio Ramen with chicken broth, pork chashu and rye noodles. Knowing I would need something to cut the broth, I added roasted tomato (highly recommend you do the same). The depth of the broth and fattiness of the pork knocked me out after all the preceding courses, leaving me to question my entire ordering strategy.

The other ramen was equally good if not better - a heat-laden red chili ramen with minced pork, smashed egg and rye noodle. The thin noodles were especially useful here, giving the broth more surface to cling to, ensuring you got a steady stream of spice after each slurp.

Wrapping Up...

This menu is packed with quality dishes and crowned by ramen that isn't messing around. You'll want to try everything (for good reason), but take it easy, be smart and recognize that you're here to taste some outstanding and unique ramen. Or don't and explore at your own pleasant peril.

OMG! No clue that ramen could even taste this good. It's conveniently located beneath me (same building) so I figured what the heck!
The broth is so flavourful and the staff is super friendly. They really make an effort to get to know you and of course I'll be coming back. Nothing like great customer service and fanatastic food :)

Very Pleasantly Surprised!  The food was delicious and the service was great.
I started with the Little Gem salad that had a Caesar vibe with a Japanese twist. Next was the vegetarian ramen which was unlike any I've ever had - the of depth of flavor was incredible- the best hands down. Love the Sorachi Ace on draft and the cool patio space. Robert, our server, was friendly and fast. Standout experience. Happy to have them in the neighborhood.

I was really pumped to try Ivan Ramen and even more excited to go on Memorial Day for dinner. I had figured people would be too busy stuffing their faces with hot dogs and burgers than to want ramen. I was right! The place was sufficiently busy but there was no wait and I was seated at the bar right away. 

The service is impeccable. Everyone is so attentive and the bartender is really on her ish. She knows everything about the menu and asked the chef [who expedites from the kitchen 2 feet away] when she didn't. 

While I thought the food was solid, the hype really inflated my expectation. Yet, I just wasn't blown away. 

Lancaster Okonomiyaki [$12]: Basically a scapple waffle with japanese mayo. I thought the flavors were a little muted. I didn't think the apple or the cabbage added any additional flavor as they were probably there to balance out the perceived saltiness of the waffle. It was still a tasty dish. 

Tokyo Shio Ramen [fully loaded, $13 + $5]: Definitely filling, I struggled to finish it. The pork chashu was really soft and tender. I enjoyed the fully loaded elements [extra pork chashu, egg, and roasted tomato], probably a little more than the ramen dish itself. Overall, the broth left a fatty/greasy taste in my mouth and was a little too salty. I found myself dying for water throughout the night. 

Tip: the roasted tomato compliments the ramen well. 

It wasn't too expensive, $32 plus tip. 

I'd give this place another try but I wouldn't wait in line to do so or call it a "ramen heaven."

This place is just okay. There wasn't a stupendous wait for a table or the food and for good reason - the ramen is mediocre.

Like other reviews have mentioned, the beauty of ramen is in the complexity of the broth. I ordered the triple garlic mazeman and the spicy red chili ramen. Both lacked depth and tasted like any ramen I could have made at home myself. Instead of boiling bone marrow to get that milky base, the restaurant merely uses a different pastes and hot water.

Love Love Love this place!! Had the pleasure of eating here tonight and was greeted by such a pleasant staff.  Everyone I walked passed was so friendly!  Our server Jillian was extremely helpful in choosing our meal pointing out what was popular and things that she really liked.  I choose the spicy chili ramen as did my friend.  Let me tell you... its been awhile since I've had ramen that when it said spicy it really was spicy and we didn't have to add anything.  The noodles were cooked a perfect al dente, and the broth was extremely flavorful.  Great food, and great service, may be my new favorite ramen shop!

Definitely, worth the hype...for the most part. Be prepared to wait, but they do have a quick turnover. You won't be waiting hours like you do at Totto or Ippudo...yet.

We started with the pork meatballs and the fried hearts & livers and both were delicious. However, we all got sick that night and we think it's from the pork meatballs being undercooked. Not a fun night...

Anyways, onto the main attraction, the ramen. I had the spicy ramen, but the rest of the table had the 4 cheese, shio and shoyu ramen. All were amazing, you won't be disappointed with any that you get. I will say, the spicy one is spicy. My friend explained it perfectly; it's too spicy to really enjoy the flavor of the noodles and broth. 

Service is great and they're very quick with the food. I will definitely be back to try a different bowl of ramen, but I'll likely skip on the appetizers....

EDIT: After posting this, the manager reached out to find out the cause of my food poisoning and basically tried to say it wasn't from him. After multiple messages back and forth, not once did he apologize for our experience until I mentioned it to him. If you have a problem with your food or experience, might be in your best interest to not mention it to them.

Like the Gotham location, the chef is a tad heavy handed with the salt on everything....and this is coming from someone who's got a very salty palate. 

We ordered the codfish liver fried rice, the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen, Spicy Red Chili Ramen and the Shoyu Ramen. They all have really good deep flavors, but I'm so overpowered by the salt that it kind of masked the good qualities of the food. 

Service was good, but I don't understand why they insisted on seating us outside at 80+ degrees when the restaurant was almost empty. We noticed they tried that with other customers too. Thank goodness we all fought for indoor seating and AC or it would've been a torturously sweaty and uncomfortable meal.

Besides Takashi's ramen, I'd have to say Ivan's is now of my favorite ramen joints. I got the Shio Ramen, fully loaded. I think it's definitely worth it to get it fully loaded. The noodles were perfectly al dente, loved the tomato and egg, and no skimpage (if that's a word) of pork. The broth was deep and flavorful and not too salty, which is hard to find! I think Momofuku's noodles are too salty, and get MSG headaches from Ippudo's ramen...
Gotham west market is great in general and definitely worth the trek!

i had first seen ivan on "mind of a chef" and was intrigued.  i wanted to check out his outpost at gotham market west when i was in NY in dec, but that was too far, so i'm glad he opened this shop in the LES.  

i shared the little gems and ankimo dirty rice w/ my friend, and both were delicious.  i just had a bite of the rice, and it was rich.

i got the shio ramen while she got the pork one.  these are not conventional ramens by any means, since hers did not really have soup.  mine was pretty light and was in a chicken-based broth w/ rye noodles.  yum!  i want to try the spicy ramen next time!

I came here on a Friday night and the place was packed. 

Ordered:

Roast pork musubi- 2 tiny pieces of roast pork on seaweed topped with a tomato. It was ok. Nothing I would do out of my way for or order again.

Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen- The noodle had that firm texture that I enjoy. I tasted bits of bacon. =) I wished the char siu was seared though. It was a decent bowl of ramen. (FYI- mazemen is brothless ramen, so don't expect a bowl of soup with that noodle)  

Overall, I had a solid meal. Though not a mind-blowing experience.

We had a long night and I was not done, I wanted to get some Ivan Ramen that was a few blocks from the hotel. We ended up driving there anyway. The restaurant was located at Clinton St. everything was closed except for a few bars and restaurants. The front of the restaurant was seat dining area and in the back was the more casual bar setting. We sat at the bar it looked like the old fashion diners with servers right on the other side taking orders. In the back of that was the window where you could see the cooks in action. Fun!  I ordered the red rice ale and the spicy red chili ramen - no kidding it was really spicy and so awesomely good! The semi-solid egg was extra but worth it! There were two kinds of noodles, the one in the broth was different from the ones that were brothless. My husband had the Four cheese mazemen (brothless) with thicker whole wheat noodles while mine was with rye noodles. They were both delicious!!

Don't bother going here.. not so special.
His ramens are not any tastier than Totto nor Momofuku nor Ippudo... I had Tokyo full on($18) & my friend Triple pork full on  ($20). w/ one beer our bill was $46. It's way too over priced. I'm very disappointed because I was excited that he was opening one in NY after watching him on mind of a chef. Ivan needs to know he can't continue his business in nyc w/ $20 ramen... something you finish eating in 5 min & leave.

Awesome place, the best ramen in the Lower East Side. We walked by, put our name down and got a text message only 20 minutes later. They sat us outside on the patio, which I didn't even know they had, and Ivan himself described each ramen dish. The food came out fast but not too fast and was all delcious. Highly recomended!!

I was in the mood for some ramen this past Friday so  I figured I would check it out. It was crowded inside but I was able to be seated quickly at the table all the way in the back. I ordered Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen- and JFC. The waiters were friendly and the atmosphere was like being at a bar with the loud music, people talking loudly and eating ramen. The noodles for my Mazemen was good but totally not work 15 dollars because I was still starving afterwards. The waiters and waitresses were standing around the cash register openly talking about how they dont like their new staff members as they walked back and forth serving customers.  I dont know about you but I enjoy eating my food without the trash talk going back and forth. There are better ramen places out there.

Went back again tonight with some other friends from school. Tried the Shoyu Ramen (fully loaded, of course), as well as the dirty rice and pickled daikon. It was just as good the second time!

The noodles in the shoyu broth were as great as in the triple pork/garlic mazemen. The pickled daikon came with some caramelized onions on top and acted as a great palate cleanser throughout the meal. The dirty rice was extremely delicious littered with succulent pieces of monkfish liver throughout. 

I sat outside this time, and while it was a bit warm, the seating was very comfortable and it was a great environment. Can't wait until they have a proper roof over the backyard! 

Thanks to Michael for a warm welcome, and it was great talking to Ivan again as well! Still strongly recommended and I'll be back again soon.

3.5 Stars

Pretty good ramen. I would say that the Mazemen outweigh the soup based ramens. The Gotham West Market location doesn't offer Mazemen so come to this one for that.

The bartender behind the counter is pretty friendly, and you might see Ivan floating around talking to customers too.

Things Ordered
Little Gem Salad - basically a reworked Caesar Salad. Pretty decent. Dressing on the salty side

Kewpie Ebi - Too much mayonnaise. Salty. But I did appreciate that prawns are served with the head.

Vegetarian Shoyu Ramen - Salty, too much soy sauce (I understand this is supposed to be Tokyo style and they like soy sauce there, but still...). Broth was sharp, not rounded. 

Spicy Red Chilli Ramen - Basically this is Mapo Tofu Ramen without the tofu. Broth again on the salty side, oily. Not really full bodied or subtle - apart from the chili and salt there's not much flavour coming through. They're not kidding about it being spicy; and it is going to kick around in your stomach. 

Tokyo Shio Ramen - Again, salty broth. Oily. Not very subtle. The smoked sea salt overwhelms the broth so there's no real chance for the the proteiny satisfaction of the broth to come through.

In the case of all three ramen, the broth:noodle ratio was off, IMO. In general, the broths are too oily, over-salted and unbalanced. The rye noodle, however, is a triumph - chewy and flavourful - and an excellent idea.

The most satisfying aspect  of the dinner was the service, which was friendly and attentive, and accommodating of requests.
I was drunk, and it was absolutely delicious. My girlfriend is family friends with Ivan, so hopefully we can catch him when he's there. Plan to go again!

a real decent bowl of ramen. definitely smaller than the standard you'd find elsewhere. the portions are a lot smaller than what they would serve in japan and that's saying a lot. 

the shoyu is great! ivan does do ramen justice. but the place is countered by a distorted experience of what a ramen shop should be. a ramen shop is where you'd go to have your quick grub and go on your way to make room for those that are waiting. yet, this place is for the typical fancy transplants. it's a bit too fancy to be a ramen shop. i can't say that this is some reappropriated white guy ramen joint since ivan did his time in japan, but it sure does feel that way!

The Ivan Ramen in Japan is really close to my house and actually Ivan is a family friend. 
Going to his ramen shop was like coming home for a bit. The flavors were unique in that they have an Ivan twist, but it was still so delicious! I can't wait to come back!

Ramen lovers, this is definitely a must visit!

A must try in les, had the pork meatballs and as expected delicious, the Tokyo shio ramen fully loaded was amazing but keep in mind it's a bit salty. the triple pork garlic mazemen was also great, no broth it's more like a sauce. Atmosphere was great and comfortable the staff were kind.
Overall a great experience.

In the past ten or so years, the availability of ramen in New York City has skyrocketed. While it may never reach the level of having multiple museums (instant and not), we have thankfully moved beyond the dark days of deifying mediocre bowls by David Chang, and are instead in the heady present of outing secret ramen pop-ups (well done, Pete) and waiting until midnight for otherwise noteworthy beef parlors to sling bowls of their own (don't bother--the richness of the broth is as terrifying as the teeth shattering fried intestines are hard). So it comes as no surprise, of course, that ramen made by a middle-aged Jewish man from Long Island was met not with trepidation, but craven anticipation. We were inundated with Eater articles, rumors fueled by the tweets of other chefs, surprise appearances at the trustafarian mecca known as Smorgasburg. There was even an entire book tour. But even inside that echo chamber of hype, where pretension and possession of knowledge of the obscure and (arguably) irrelevant are points of pride, few truly knew the background of the man behind the craze: Ivan Orkin. 

"He sounds Russian. Doesn't he? Wasn't there an Ivan in...some Rocky movie?" asked the diminutive blonde coupled up a few tables down, in between furtively poking her thousand year old deviled eggs with her chopsticks. In truth, Mr. Orkin could almost be considered Japanese. This isn't simply by virtue of time spent in the country (though it is considerable, having taught English there throughout the 1980s and having moved back in the early 2000s before returning to New York, last year) but also stems from the impressive asceticism of his cooking. His ramens are not the debilitating gut-bombs of yesteryear, gleaming with collagen and redolent of pork belly - they are very nearly insouciant, subtle yet distinct, each component falling harmoniously into line, rather than competing to be the loudest. That approach extends to all of his cooking, appetizers included. This is asceticism not to the rigidity of a cuisine but to the fidelity of ingredients. Take the "Lancaster Okonomiyaki," for instance. Okonomiyaki is the giant pancake filled with cabbage and pork (typically) topped with shaved bonito and scallions that you drunkenly order at an izakaya after one too many beers and a few too many moments of staring at the tauntingly glossy menu pictures. Okonomiyaki is also considered a Japanese quintessential comfort food on the level of curry or yakisoba. so - while the ability to top it with almost anything is liberating - the idea of changing the base recipe, in this case the batter, in any way is almost sacrosanct. The batter gets its trademark fluffiness from the inclusion of yamaimo, a Japanese mountain yam that's so unnaturally sticky and slimy when handled and grated that it makes raw okra look appealing. Instead of a batter filled with pork, the Lancaster Okonomiyaki is made of scrapple, cutting out the middle man. And yet, the meat is nearly as springy as the batter would have been. The charred cabbage gives a hint of smoky bitterness, while the pickled Fuji apples and maple-infused Kewpie (a Japanese brand of mayonnaise that's somehow both mild in flavor but substantial in body) add sweet and sour notes in equal measure, resulting in a dish you'll likely finish before it ever cools down to the "Warm" title it's listed under. The "Roast Pork Musubi" is equally adventurous, and equally successful. Rather than the requisite sliver of Spam, tightly wound tendrils of pork are dolloped unto a loose smattering of rice on a sheet of nori, before being topped with a quiveringly soft ball of roasted tomato. The tomato is darkly sweet, like a brick red smear of molasses, enhancing and enriching the salty, unctuous pork. The nutty, toasty profile of the nori and the light vinegar coating the rice glide through the background, bringing together an incredibly balanced series of bites. It is regrettable, then, that all of the ramen is not as exciting in comparison.

It is fitting in a restaurant festooned with a wall collage of odes to Japanophilia that the menu would include at least one head-scratcher. The "Four Cheese Mazemen," like many dishes that has "Four Cheese" in the title, quickly devolved into a goopy, indistinct, rapidly congealing mess. The pickled bean sprouts lacked the punch to cut through much of anything, let alone the titanic richness of the cheese. The dashi is lost at this particular sea as well, its briny profile never rising from the curd laced depths. The otherwise excellent noodles bumble through this slog like Adam West's Batman, only your bowl doesn't come adorned with comic book noises scrawled in katakana. His best are his classics: shio and tonkotsu, both leading sensory returns to Tokyo, both showing the finesse and depth of flavor his style is capable of. Take the opportunity to eat here before the hype reconstitutes - you haven't got long.

I decided to give this place another shot even though I had a mediocre meal the first time around. I came for dinner last night and it was definitely as underwhelming as I remember.

We got there around 8:45 and were seated immediately. We split the Lancaster Okonomiyaki and JFC to start,  and I ordered the Tokyo Shio Ramen.

JFC consists of double dredged chicken hearts and livers, with a ponzu honey mustard dipping sauce.  I can't say that I normally eat innards so I don't really know what textures and flavors I was expecting but all of these were so bland. I couldn't really make out what I was eating.  They were fried perfectly --super crispy, but needed seasoning. The inside was rather mushy and tasteless. The innards seemed to be the vehicle to highlight the ponzu honey mustard, which was way too strong and overwhelming.


The Lancaster Okonomiyaki was excellent. It's made of a scrapple waffle topped with charred cabbage, pickled apple and maple kewpie. I expected the waffle to be meatier but it wasn't. Although the whole thing is just fillers..the ratio definitely favored the doughier components. Still wonderful though. It was mushy but a good tasty mush, with a crispy exterior a waffle should have. The cabbage and kewpie on top was familiar and delicious. The pickled apple was a tad too tart for me so I picked those out.

The Tokyo Shio Ramen(sea salts, dashi + chicken broth, pork chashu, rye noodle) was so disappointing. The noodles were actually really good, perfectly firm and chewy. But, the broth was so bland(what happened to the sea salt? !) and ridiculously oily. With each slurp of noodles,  my lips were coated in a film of oil, ugh. The chashu was also terrible. Extremely fatty, no flavor. Booo!

The appetizers, specifically the okonomiyaki and ankimo dirty rice I had the first time, are great and probably the only items I would order again if I happen to come back. Otherwise, I'll be heading to Minca a few blocks over to get my ramen fix.

There has been so much press regarding this place that it's easy to look at it with a jaundiced eye, but I found there was no need for such skepticism. Being a fairly adventurous eater, I was excited to see the option of the JFC appetizer - crispy chicken hearts and livers with a ponzu honey sauce. Good stuff. For the entree, I advocate going with the triple pork triple garlic mazemen. Not only do you get a tender and flavorful char siu, but you're also privy to a healthy sprinkling of bacon bits. To counteract the pork overdose, the dish is laden with fresh bean sprouts. Be aware, mazemen differs from normal ramen in that there's really no broth here. I think the noodles are cooked in a tonkotsu broth to give them flavor, but there's nothing to slurp. Knowing that, I opted to get the egg and roasted tomato add-ons so that I could mix them in with the noodles in order to retain some liquid-like consistency. The chili oil also helps with this, so don't be too shy to ask for it. And its potency is no joke - quite spicy. My only disappointment was the interesting sounding yuzu lemonade; I suggest skipping this, as it tasted like plain old lemonade to me. Service was a plus, as Jillian's pleasant and friendly demeanor in spite of the active Thursday night crowd was quite welcome.

I really enjoyed Ivan Ramen! I was really happy Ivan offered a vegetarian Ramen option. The Japanese cannot comprehend ramen without meat and veggie ramen practically does not existent in Japan. Since my trip to Japan last month I have been on the hunt for New York's best Japanese restaurants. Ivan Ramen is a great edition to lower Manhattan and I recommend it highly. Cant wait to go back.

Great new spot in LES!

Pros:
-Delicious Ramen.  I mean it.  Egg was perfect, pork divine.  Broth was thicker than what I am used to but so flavorful.
-Decor-so fun, airy, and loads of space.  A nice departure from the 10 seat ramen joints a lot of us might be used to.  Made for only a 10 minute wait on a Thursday night.
-Drinks-Nice variety of sakes, beers, and wines.

Con:
-Portion size.  Small...I never finish my meal, and have a relatively small appetite, but I finished my whole bowl plus appetizer, and my husband was left wanting a whole additional bowl!

All in all, solid ramen spot and worth trying!!

I came with E and E can't handle spicy food, and so I ended up ordering the following.

Kewpie Ebi
fried whole prawns, smoked chili, watercress, lemon - okay this sounded like it would be good, but totally should have put two and two together. Kewpie - hellos, that is mayo. This was too much for me. It would be good without the mayo and just seasoned a different way. It wasn't good at all.


Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen
tonkotsu broth, pork chashu, whole wheat noodle - since I couldn't get the Spicy ramen again, because of E, I decided to get this one and this wasn't bad at all. I still like the Spicy Ramen the best.

I'll be back to eat an entire bowl myself.

Had Ivan Ramen for dinner with friends on a Friday night and during dinner time so the wait was expected.  We waited around 45 minutes.  Apparently they don't take reservations but you can come a bit early and put your name on the waiting list, they'll text or/and call you once your table is ready.

I had the  Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen.  Good broth, excellent ramen noodles, great texture and freshness.  

I like the lively atmosphere, the space itself was good and airy for New York.  I would come back here.  Overall a great experience!

TIP:  ADD EGG! :)

This place was absolutely delicious. As an appetizer, I had the fried chicken hearts and liver. The only complaint I have about that was the amount of bread they used for that small heart. For entree, I got the Tokyo Shio Ramen, which was amazing. I would definitely recommend and this is quite possibly the best ramen I've ever had.

Previously went to the slurp shop, which i have written a review about. I am also a fan of this joint, which is closer to me and ironically it's easier to find a parking spot in LES vs hell's kitchen. This place opened in May according to the staff and The menu looks more expanded here, which i settled w/ the braised ox tongue and tempura chicken liver & heart. Also went all out w/ fully loaded shio ramen, which is $5 extra and pretty steep for a bowl of ramen at $18 total. (I've also had their chilli hot ramen before, which is pretty hot just as a warning.) Pretty solid and consistent with what i come to know from the slurp shop. The place is decent size, similar to other places in LES, railroad style w/ a bar in the back. Can see this place with a decent wait during peak hours. Will serve as a good downtown option for me close to brooklyn.

Trying the new Ramen place on my street. I was curious if it's anywhere near as good as the places you have to wait 30 min for. 

The deviled egg was really good.  $3 good? Honestly yes. I was however shocked just how very cup-o-noodles their ramen was. They weren't quite that bad, but it was like they were using that as the standard. I've had ramen in good places in New York and Little Tokyo LA, I know what I'm talking about. These made regular ramen look like udon. The menu said it already had some pork in it without being "fully loaded" for $5 more,  but it was this over boiled gross hunk I would have mistaken for tofu if not for the strip of gristle attached to it. 

The atmosphere is nice,  wallpaper seems to have been done in the same vein as Vaselka's, semi-ironic images of people (and such) enjoying their food to varying degrees of emphasis. Lots and lots of seating, and a funky outdoor area in back. The manager sure likes 80s classic rock music. I guess that's a nice break if you're used to j-pop in these places. Hey I'm not complaining, I grew up with the Pretenders. Service was pleasant and speedy. 

Idk I mean it's not terrible but at these prices,  I expect a bit more than something I can get in a Styrofoam cup for 50¢. I think I'll stick to the joints on St Marks Place.

We read the reviews and it sounded like it would be a long wait but it was pretty easy to get a table.  Interesting interiors.  Looked like an okay porch in the back but we sat at the bar.  At the waitresses' recommendation, we ordered lancaster okonomiyaki, the triple pork triple garlic mazemen and the spicy red chili ramen.  The lancaster okonomiyaki was under cooked, so my girlfriend didn't like it but I thought it was okay, so finished it for her.  The garlic mazemen was good but the spicy ramen was not.  I like spicy food but I found this sort of offensive as the heat was overpowering without a good flavor.  Probably the best thing we had was the yuzu lemonade.  I love ramen and live in the neighborhood, so was really hoping that this would work out but after $65 (!) for a below par experience, we probably won't go back.  Too bad.

Ate at the bar here during weekday dinner. 

It's a fancy diner, basically, and the presiding idea is that its taking back ramen as comfort food. Had the triple pork/triple garlic tonkatsu mazemen. It's a thick broth (and less of it, but that's by design) served with wheat noodles, a big, buttery (floppy) piece of chashu and crumbled bacon. It was appropriate portioned, served steaming hot (the way I like it), boldly flavored and fantastically textured. 

Also tried my gf's soy ramen and it was pretty good. Glassy noodles, a thinner broth than I like but tasty. Aside from the chashu (same kind as above) and some seaweed, the stuff (like boiled egg) that you'd expect in more traditional ramen had to be purchased as an add-on. She skipped the extras and still enjoyed her bowl. 

The Tofu Coney Island's best bit was the actual tofu, which was golden and crisp. The mushroom chili was a just kind of too intensely salty when combined with the yellow mustard. 

If you're game to try a whimsical take on ramen, you'll be very satisfied, but if you're looking for roots ramen it might be better to try elsewhere.

So... I'm a big fan of ramen, and I'm big fan of Tokyo, and I'm a big fan of Mind of a Chef, so by logical reason, I should be a big fan of ramen prepared by a chef who got his start in the ramen in business in Tokyo and who was featured in Mind of a Chef. It's not that it was bad, it's just that this place is the perfect example of a restaurant that didn't live up to the hype (or price). 

Came here with a group of 3 around 7:00 on a Thursday night and were seated immediately. Having read about issues getting a table, I was surprised as the place was basically only half full the whole time we were there. 

We shared a bunch of appetizers, and sorta, not really shared our ramen dishes. 

Pickled daikon with dried shrimp - this was a surprisingly good dish. Daikon had nice flavor, and the dried shrimp, normally a very pungent ingredient, was fried and crisp which both took off the abrasive edge, and most of the flavor. It more less turned it into a crunchy topping with no seafood flavor. Still good, but any bit of shrimp essence there was lost. 

1000 year old deviled egg - having had 1000 year old egg multiple times in Asia, I can tell you from experience, this is not 1000 year old egg. It is a deviled egg, nothing more, and nothing special at all. As these were 2 eggs to an order and there were three of us, we asked for an extra egg. We were denied. Apparently putting a third egg on the plate and charging an extra $1.75 is too much effort; we were told we needed 2 orders. Instant -1 star for a lack of accommodation for a very simple request. 

JFC - I couldn't tell which pieces were hearts and which were livers. It's a good dish, if you are into fried, soft meats, but not a must have by any means. 

Lancaster Okonomiyaki - having had both waffles and scrapple, this had the texture of neither, which is the best part of both. The flavors were scrapple for sure, but it was soft and soggy. Had this been dropped in a deep fried after cooking to crisp it up, it would have been awesome. 

Triple pork / garlic mazemen - to me, the best ramen dish and noodles of the night. The noodles are a little thicker here than the other ramens we had, and are awesome. The noddles are exactly how you want them: thick and chewy. The sauce was thick and rich. The main complaint here is that you get one tiny slice of pork chashu. One. At any other ramen place you get easily 4 times the pork. With the egg, it was an $18 dish. Sorry, not worth it for what it was. 

Shoyu ramen - this, and the spicy ramen, had much thinner noodles, which frankly, just weren't anything special. The broth tasted thin in flavor. Honestly it was like a wonton soup broth with soy sauce. 

Spicy red chili ramen - noodles, see above in the shoyu ramen. This is spicy, but the broth gets more complex as you go down. The top is super spicy, and one flavor, but as the dish goes on, the broth becomes thicker... Almost creamy, and all the delicious meaty bits collect at the bottom of the bowl. That's the money spot. 

Total came to $55 per person for he above, plus 4 drinks, and including a 20% and tax. For the quality of the food and the price, I'd recommend sticking with Ippudo or Totto Ramen (in that order).  If you come, I recommend the pickled daikon, pork mazemen, and spicy ramen. Like I said, it wasn't bad. It just didn't come close to living up to the hype, or the price for what it was. Extra minus for not being able to serve an extra egg when asked.

I've never really been sure what entitles a ramen place to charge $14 for a small bowl of ramen. The best places I've been have, if they charged that much, filled me up for hours. I came here hungry and left...feeling like I could have eaten more. The ramen was certainly delicious with a great aroma, but it was a limited menu and each bowl had very limited toppings included in the price (one medium-sized piece of pork, a few beansprouts, seaweed)- another thing that was annoying. 

It's very small in here and there is certainly a rushed feel, but I can't complain about the actual decor or service.

Overall, I don't feel that my experience would warrant a return.
Very friendly staff. The Spicy Red Chili ramen is a delightful Hell-broth. You just pray this place isn't overtaken by people who talk about Lena Dunham and organic socks.

This is not your everyday, "I've got a craving for ramen and I need something quick and satisfying" kind of place. But it's good to switch things up sometimes. 

Husband and I opted for the beef tongue, Chinese broccoli, and scrapple waffle for starters. Between two people the tongue and waffle were a little rich so the astringent broccoli dish was much appreciated. Whoever thought of putting scrapple on a waffle iron and topping with a slaw, bravo. More things in life should incorporate scrapple or be served in waffle form. 

Our entrees were the chili ramen and triple pork triple garlic mazeman "fully loaded" (with roasted tomato and egg). To be fair the waiter warned us the chili ramen was 8/10 spicy and I could only tolerate a sip of the broth. Husband ate as much as he could and was sweating profusely from the spice (and he NEVER sweats... Weird Asians). 

The mazeman was really rich and perfectly sized portion. Chewy, whole wheat noodles, a thick, slightly sweet porky glaze, fatty pork belly, and crispy bacon compose the dish. I love an egg with my ramen but maybe it was a bit too much. The roasted tomato definitely enhanced though. Would've love it piping hot but the pork and egg were room temperature. Is that how it's supposed to be and I just don't know?

Other details: You can sit inside at a long row of tables with a cute decoupaged mural of pop art, or outside in the garden. There's only one unisex bathroom. They serve booze. People started lining up around 5:15 on a Sunday when we went (they don't open til 5).

Don't know if my review will be posted, but I just finished my hot chili ramen at the original Ivan ramen in setagaya Ku, Tokyo.  It's on a very local street that you would be hard pressed to ever find, so it's mostly just college aged young people eating after work.  

The place is one counter long. You order from the vending machine! Shio, hot, miso (in winter only) or agadashi. Behind the counter is a room where they make the ramen. On the other end is the pork roaster. In between is where they compose each bowl.  No hype, just clean flavorful, al dente noodles, and a nice broth, and some fresh watercress-like greens.  The three of us slurped up the whole thing in under 20 minutes, and left satisfied. It's actually a great, ordinary experience that I wish New Yorkers had the chance to appreciate. Oh yes, the bowls ranged from $8.50 to $9.50. The only reason I didn't rate it five, was I could have used a little more broth and a few more noodles.

Very friendly and great service. However, the two ramen bowls we ordered: vegetarian and chicken broth based were both very heavy on the sodium. Though
tasty, the saltiness was accosting. We would not go back, and prefer the other well-known ramen place in Hells Kitchen.

I went there on a date with my gf.  

I ordered the Spicy Ramen.

It was flavorful but a bit too spicy. 

It gave me diarrhea.  

The end.

Ivan's official NYC flagship restaurant has made me a believer, finally.  Having had a rather lackluster experience at the Slurp Shop at Gotham West Market - I must admit that I felt slight trepidation coming here.  However, all my expectations were exceeded and my doubts erased.  Anticipating a long wait around 7:15pm on a Saturday, the bf and I actually had no wait at all. Better yet, we even snagged a nice little two-top in the back patio on a warm summer evening. Service was also efficient, cordial and very professional throughout the meal, definitely a pleasant surprise for a ramen shop.

Now let's get down to the food ordered:
- Pickled daikon XO - consisted of thinly shaved daikon topped with plenty of savory dried shrimp and scallop in an XO chili oil.  While XO sauce is typically used in Cantonese cuisine, I liked how the salty, funky flavor mixed with the acidic daikon.  Not only was it a good dish to whet the appetite, but also provided nice acidity in between bites of ramen.
- Lancaster okinomiyaki - a small okinomiyaki made with scrapple, charred cabbage, pickled apples, drizzled with maple kewpie. I am a big fan of traditional okinomiyaki, but found this version to be even better because it was less doughy and more filled with sweet, sour and salty components. This is the perfect little Jewish/Japanese snack.
- Shoyu ramen, fully loaded - we steered clear of the mazemen during this visit due to a less than perfect experience with it at Slurp Shop, which turned out to be a good call.  I loved the springy rye noodles, while the soy sauce chicken dashi had just the right amount of salt. The roasted tomato was a surprising twist, but everything came together well.

Ivan Ramen is definitely a welcomed addition to the already amazing NYC ramen scene. What makes this place really stand out for me though, is that the menu offers so much more than just ramen. Will be back soon!

Ok so first things first, don't ever let anyone tell you that cheese and pickled vegetables taste good together because they do not. I ordered the cheese mazemen because it was a hot day and I didn't want soup. My friend got the triple pork mazemen so I decided to order the only other mazemen option. I'd heard great things about a slice of cheese on top of instant ramen so I thought that this dish would be inventive and fun. Unfortunately I was wrong but luckily my friends were generous enough to share parts of their amazing dishes. The aforementioned triple pork had just the right amount of salt and seasoning and the texture of the noodles were perfect unlike mine which were drenched with an exorbitant amount of melted cheese. 
The real star was the cold broth ramen with rye noodles and mackerel. The mackerel piece was huge and so fresh and perfectly flaky and the mackerel infused broth was strong but also light and refreshing at the same time. The rye noodles were chewy and nutty, a perfect complement to the cool and salty broth. Simply amazing. 
We also shared the sriracha fried shrimp and the okonomiyaki to start but neither of them were especially amazing for me
Light broth and succulent chasu pork, brings us back to Tokyo where we lived for 5 years.

Was put off by their wait list system which can be a bit infuriating when you see so many empty seats - they just don't do a good job of filling seats quickly.  They also overestimated our wait time by an hour. 

Enjoyed seeing Ivan at his shop but he didn't do much in the way of building a rapport with his customers. 

The definitive item on this menu is the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen.  A rich and tasty dish.  The other winner at the table was the Dirty Monkfish Rice.  
Other dishes ordered include the Cheese Mazemen (good but very one-noted) and the Spicy Ramen (too salty).

I had hesitations at coming to the sit-down location for Ivan Ramen, especially given the less-than-awesome experience I had at their Gotham West Market location, however I'm really glad my second experience turned out significantly better than the first.

One of the less than stellar points of the evening was the flack I received at getting a table. At 6pm on a Thursday evening, the restaurant was all but deserted, yet they told me I needed to wait for the rest of my party to arrive before I could be seated. They conceded in letting me sit down once I told them my friend was less than five minutes away -- but even so, I was really nervous until she arrived, because what if the restaurant suddenly filled up and I was holding up a table someone else could have and... seriously, are those the feelings a restaurant wants to evoke in a customer?

We started off with the Lancaster okonomiyaki, which is a scrapple waffle drizzled with maple-laced kewpie mayo, pickled apple bits, and charred cabbage. Being a fan of scrapple from my days in Pennsylvania, I thoroughly enjoyed this take on the okonomiyaki.

My friend wasn't completely thrilled by her bowl of shio ramen, but I don't think that's the feature dish of Ivan Ramen -- personally, the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen is. I loved every single bite of this, especially the fact that this wasn't overly heavy given the scorching day outside. The bacon bits were a bit too distracting, but the garlicky sauce and the perfectly chewy noodles were amazing. I can't wait to come back for more of this!

Noodles: 
Ivan's signature rye ramen noodles were different than the usual ramen noodles found in other shops. They were fine, done al-dente and was a nice change. They reminded me a bit of Chinese wonton noodles in terms of their consistency. I think I still prefer the usual ramen noodles however. I got the Shio ramen and the (chicken) broth was quite light and delicious, I drank up the entire bowl! My friend is vegetarian and has always had problems finding vegetarian ramen in Toronto, where we are from. She loved her first ramen experience! I tasted a bit of her shitake mushroom broth and found it to be quite deliciou

Apps: The best part of our meal, was the tofu cubes. Our waiter described it as Coney island style chill 'fries', except the fries = cubes of deep fried firm tofu. It was to die for. I would return just for that small dish! We were told that the pork meatballs were great too, but we didn't get a chance to try it. 

Service: was great! We were told originally an hour wait on Saturday at 8pm. They take your phone # and text you when the table is ready. I have a Toronto number so I was a bit nervous about not getting a text so I went back and checked at the 30 min mark, our table was ready! I did not receive a text even though they said they had texted the correct number. Good thing we checked!

Not sure if I would return since I'm not in NYC too often, i think next time I would try a different ramen place such as Totto! We liked Ippudo's ramen better.

More than a ramen shop! They have pretty good appetizers so you don't have to just get ramen. Got their musubi and dirty rice and they were both delicious. The dirty rice was a bit oily but I didn't mind it much because I love monkfish liver and it just tasted so good. Their garlic ramen mazemen was delicious but I felt it was pricey at $15. It didn't have much stuff in it. Got their spicy ramen which was pretty spicy like people said. I was still able to eat it but not drink the broth much. I didn't really like this though, because it was all spicy flavor and nothing else. The noodles were thin and overdone. Do not recommend the spicy ramen. 

I'm surprised there so much seating in this ramen location! There's even outdoor seating.

got tokyo shoyu ramen and spicy red chili ramen....w.t.f. this is not ramen. tasted like shit. tokyo shoyu was hella salty that I had to add some water then it was edible. the spicy red chili was really spicy and the soup was really oily and just...ew
never coming back. terrible and rude workers. waitress was nice but the others were rude.

Tried out the brick and mortar Ivan Ramen shop and compared to their Market west booth location this definitely has more options. Wonderful drinks as their ivan iced tea and lemonade were refreshing.

Besides the ramen they had great appetizers. A whole fried shrimp, crispy and juicy with a nice spicey kick. Definitely the shrimp heads were a delight. A wonderful picked daikon with xo sauce. The ramen to me was a bit salty but the rye noodles are a surprise which i liked. If you are here go with the shio. Wonderfully cooked egg with a soft center. Overall a bit pricey for the options and food you get that doesn't stand out. For me it would be a one time visit.

Not your usual traditional Japance Ramen place - more fusion / modern / urban aesthetic (like, if Steve Aoki opened a Ramen joint, I'd imagine Ivan). Came here on a Saturday night, party of 3 and expected to wait but was seated immediately (just good luck/timing - the place was packed). The 1000 year deviled egg wasn't actually as weird as it sounds (tasted like a regular devilled egg with hints of 1000 year egg flavoring). The dirty rice is as delicious as everyone says - we split the dish and finished every grain. I got the veggie ramen, which had arugula and roasted tomato - I really enjoyed it and thought it blended well. Their poached egg was perfect. I would go back for sure

Why, hello skinny non-Asian people who want to serve me ramen. What a bright and colorful, animated restaurant you have. 

I like it.

Although narrow when you first walk in, it opens up in the back into a wider room with a counter for solo's & bigger tables for non-dates. There is also an outside dining area. Our waitress was so happy and all-smiles, I think she really did make the experience a lot better. 

I dared to venture and try the ridiculously red spicy ramen. Now, THIS is what spicy ramen should taste like. Although I'm not a fan of the rye noodles, the broth was painfully delicious. I was a bit sad that not much came in it and I would have to pay for add-ons. It is what it is.

I have been to Ivan Ramen twice, and have  gotten the Shoyu ramen and the Shio ramen. While I enjoyed the Shio more, both were very good. Ivan ramen is very minimalist- do not come expecting a bowl filled with forn mushrooms and lots of meat. However, this sparing approach has resulted in the essential elements treated with utmost care. Both The noodles and the broth are unique and flavorful. My only complaint was that there was not very much meat- only one largeish piece.

I have not ordered any of the appetizers, but the barley iced tea is very good.

Walked into Ivan Ramen on a Thursday evening and was greeted by super nice hosts and waiters. They told me there was no wait and was seated right away. 

I wanted to try the seasonal cucumber lemonade which was flavorful and perfect for a warm summer night. 

We started with the 1000 Year Deviled Egg that tastes of Bonito fish and a creamy yolk fill. Maybe the saltiness is supposed to be reminisce of 1000 Year eggs but I didn't get any of that. Maybe that's a good thing. I'm not sure how preserved egg flavors would translate in this setting. 

Of course we had to get the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen and the Spicy Red Chili Ramen. The noodles were cooked perfectly in both but the former had thicker noodles than the latter. 

The Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen was full of flavor. Make sure you mix the noodles around the bowl after every bite to get everything in each bite. The only thing is that they should've maybe cut up the pork belly slice so it would mix well and easier to eat than a whole strip in your bowl. Grabbing the last few bits and some of the broth on the bottom was the best part. I thought I would miss the lack of broth in this dish but the thickness of the 'soup' that was there coats the noodles well and helps to adhere pork bits and garlic bits into every bite. 

The Spicy Red Chili Ramen was pretty spicy. Definately a back of the throat peppery backbone with a bright overall flavor profile almost reminding me of a Buffalo sauce (as in Buffalo Wings). The egg and pork really holds this dish together. For such a bold flavored dish, I wish the ramen was a bit thicker however. 

Overall a nice innovative ramen shop. They are far from your classic ramen but love what they've done.

The tokyo shio ramen didn't really do it for me. The broth was a little too rich without enough going on flavor-wise. I'm down to give Ivan a second change but it was hard to get a sense for what the hype was about. I will say the texture of the noodles was great though.

The crispy pork meatballs are pretty good. Incredibly soft on the inside.
I was really good. I'm not a ramen fan in general, so I was a fan of the americanized version

I think this is a place to be tried - i just don't know if it lived up to its hype. 

1 - We had to sit inside, because the wait for an outdoor table was 20 mins. Inside is kinda hustle-bustle, non-relaxed.  Felt industrial. 

2 - I had the triple pork, triple garlic mazeman and thought it was delicious, but mainly because it tasted like a buttery, bacon infused, super salty pasta. Not difficult to make this amount of fat and salt taste amazing, you know?
