Drinks selection extensive, some good apple ciders and beers that rotate. I got a cold brew coffee but for some reason they were out of milk for a Sunday brunch which was a bit off-putting, ended up just having it with some liquid syrup. 

We got the daikon with XO sauce as the appetizer and that was our highlight - delicious, sour daikon pickles topped with this great minced meat sauce with a funky, fish sauce-like taste, very unique and really had us wishing for more.

I got the spicy chicken ramen, quite spicy (probably 7/10 for people that like spicy food), quite good but a bit lacking in ingredients; the chicken and vegetables were reduced down into the sauce and had me digging around looking for some solid bits for a while.

The traditional soy sauce ramen (Shoyu) was disappointing versus what you can get at Totto or Hide-Chan, way too salty and only had a single piece of Chashu pork in it. Didn't think it was worth the money or the wait.

The breakfast/brunch menu was interesting, someone in our party got the omelette which was OK, we didn't try the buckwheat pancakes but these sounded somewhat intriguing as well.

All in all, the ramen was OK, prices were a bit on the high side for ramen, and probably worth skipping for one of the more recognized ramen places you can find in NYC.

first off, I eat alot of ramen. I've been trying to go to every ramen place in the city. so far, nothing beats ippudo. anyway, decided to try Ivan after hearing great reviews. We got here, the waitress gives us the menu and my girl orders the triple garlic ramen and i order the shio ramen. The waitress takes our order and goes. In the meantime, we see a "white" couple come in and sit behind us. The waitress decides to chat them up. Oh you should add a egg with your ramen. This goes well with this that goes well with that. I was looking at my girl thinking... wtf? Mine is just plain ramen. Why didnt she tell me to add anything extra? really? I dont want to complain about racism these days but seriously? 

I'm not really sure what to think about this place.... but with so many different options in the city this place is def not worth it.

I ordered Shyo yiu ramen and my friend ordered spicy ramen.
Noodles are ok. But both soups are not impressive.
maybe I should try the apptizers i will feel better.

Ivan Ramen is, to me, is a prime example of what it means to be a New Yorker, and New York life: 
we have delicious Japanese ramen with an American- even Jewish twist, with a side of NYC styled ultra-gentrificaion, WHILE tasting pretty darned good!

Its unusual to find a chicken based ramen... anywhere. Anywhere but Ivan Ramen. Chicken fat (or in Yiddish, schmaltz)+ ramen? Yes... lets secretly feed people Jewish food under the guise of 'fusion'. I love it! Plus, it tastes great! Yes, the broth could do with more of that thick collagen thats more readily found in pork and beef bones, but this stuff is just as good.

I didn't ask the waiter if Ivan Ramen uses happy animals (pasture raised, cage-free, access to outdoors, prison-free life style animals) but assumed they didn't and asked if I could replace the pork in my dish with tofu. Turns out they don't carry tofu. WTF? How on earth do you not have tofu at an asian fusion place?! But instead they replaced the pork with some delicious enoki mushroom and I was just as pleased. There are some plates where the meat add-on takes the cake of the dish, thus by removing it you are leaving the dish bland, sad, and without a soul. However, the broth (that jewish-delight broth!) was the star quarterback of the ramen, and any add-ons or take aways affects the dish in an unnoticeable fashion.

but wait, lets return to this no tofu business. How on earth do you not carry tofu in a asian fusion restaurant? Whats next? Soy sauce?! You, Mr. Asian Fusion, are you going to tell me, Ms. Asian Person no tofu? Coming into my territory and taking away a core of my people's culture? 
This.... is where I can't tell if its a hilarious comment on NYC columbus-ification or is this really outrageous.... and also, k'mon, we are in LES! The heart of a latino/black low income community now equipped with a pricy ramen shop! is this gentrification.... or is this really-- naw, its really gentrification at its finest. 

if you come in ravenous, be prepared to fill up with ramen + a couple of sides. A bowl of hearty ramen won't fill you up if you're belly needs a fill'in. 

either way, this shits delicious. Ive eaten many-a-bowl here. Be daring. Try that cheese ramen. Its good.

I know that I should rave about their ramen but I find that the notable dishes are found in their small bites, especially the pork meatballs. Price is pricey for a ramen shop.

Great service, love the staff there.

This is not ramen. It's rye noodles in soy sauce water. Never trust a white guy with ramen. 13 bucks for a bowl is absurd. It only comes with a small piece of dry pork. Better take the train down to momofuku instead. You can thank me later.

I had the Shoyu Ramen with mushrooms. Really yummy especially if you like salty, it is a soy sauce/chicken dashi (broth).
The daikon starter with shrimp sauce was a great starter and accompaniment.
The wait staff was very friendly and attentive as well.

The food is good, and fairly priced. The ramen isn't authentic and it doesn't pretend to be. If you've ever craved the sacrilegious marriage between Japanese style noodles and American comfort food, this is the place for you!

Cheddar mac-n-cheese ramen is a go.

The place was ok, nothing that special. The buyer should beware! We ordered the PORK ribs and we did not ask about the price and the server did not offer the price either.  Needless to say, we were shocked, when the billed arrived and the ribs were $42.00. We paid and on the way out spoke to manger, about our experience, and his only reply was to say "the server did not mention the price."  The manager, did not seem surprised by this issue and he also did not seem to care.  In the end, a very disappointing experience.

I've finally come to the conclusion that there are no good ramen places in the Lower East side. Ramen $15, plus $3 for extra chasu. The thing comes in a small bowl with 3 small slices of pork. Isn't the chasu supposed to be like the ones in the buns? Round? 

So without the extra pork, would it have come with ONE slice of pork? Also, it didn't seem like they used the blowtorch on the pork. The soup was meh...had to dump in their hot sauce to even make it tasty. 

It was basically just soy sauce soup with noodles, one boiled egg, thin pork slices and some shaved veggie. Where's the seaweed? Numerous other ingredients missing. If you want good ramen go to Totto Ramen on 52nd street. PERIOD. Their mega bowl for about $15 comes with at least 5 or 6 pieces of chasu and it's fully loaded. Their regular bowl for about $10 is still amazing. It's spicy (they actually have chili oil that's tasty). All in all, for $23....not impressed at all! 

I should have known when I saw a white cook in the kitchen. No offense but I want my Indian food cooked by Indians and my ramen made by Japanese people.

Agreed the small bites is what I wanted to take the most bites of. Very challenging menu to negotiate being GF and vegetarian. These options are not clearly demarkartef on the menu or by service( minus 1 star). Otherwise service was prompt and friendly. I was hoping for standout flavors and they were more comfort food flavors .... Which is traditional ramen!  So, meh. Fair for a one off!

Thought I would give the LES location a try after not really liking the service at Slurp Shop. 

Opentable reservation made it easy but we didn't need it this Sunday night. The front was empty but the bar area was happening with two seats for us. 

Coney Island tofu came out piping hot, the miso mushroom chili is an awesome topping which simulates that of real meat cili, the onions and scallions add a great taste and crunch.

The vegatarian ramen comes out looking like a garden but don't be fooled the broth is hearty and umami.  My spicy red chili ramen was not for the weak, much more spicier than the first time I had it.

My husband loved the rye noodles but I prefer a chewier, thicker noodle.

In a nutshell: overpriced average ramen.
We made a reservation for 8 people Saturday evening and were pleasantly surprised when we were seated outside in the courtyard. It was a bit tight but we made it work. The ramen menu is pretty standard, and they had a special of scallops. My friend and I decided to order the special and the shoyu ramen to split. 
The entree size is quite small. The scallop "entree" turned out to be 6 raw scallops (which I don't think the waitress told us) with some salmon roe and that was it. It being $16 and an entree, I expected it to be more. When the waitress introduced it as "perfect for a summer day like today" I expected something light but not something appetizer-sized. The ramen bowl is smaller than what you would expect too. The dashi in the shoyu ramen was tasty and I wish there was more. I asked others later on what they thought of the portion size and everyone agreed it was on the smaller side. Probably won't return again as there are other and better ramen places in NYC.

There's a lot of hype here, and I think it's probably worth it. 

I've only been for lunch, and the menu has changed all three times. Never had to wait during the weekday lunch hour. 

Spicy ramen is solid; noodles aren't too al dente (I'm looking at you, Ippudo)  Pork meatballs are so soft and excellent. Roast Pork Masubi is like sushi, but it's soft roasted pork so it's better. They put a couple of sandwiches on the lunch menu, Herbie's International blew our minds. Pork was so soft, roll was fresh and perfect. Shoyu ramen is OK; not spicy so perhaps that's why I didn't LOVE it. Dan Dan noodles exploded with flavor, but the #1 Dan Dan dish is at Han Dynasty...

The only thing I wouldn't get again was this prawn in chili sauce over kale. Only a few prawns on a bed of kale, which isn't ideal because, well, it's kale.

Love this place. 

Innovative and fresh Japanese-American fusion. 

Can't go wrong with the Prickly Pear Lemonade. It's bright pink!

Really overpriced given the menu. Even lunch is $15+ for basic (and super salty) Ramen and the add-ons will put you in the $25 area. I ate here for dinner and wasn't wowed but figure I give them a 2nd shot. 

Nah, not at these prices, I'm surprised they don't charge for tap water. Feels like I'm paying the rent instead of noodles. I blame Clinton St, they have the highest turnover on this block. Just don't feel like spending $30 for lunch. Sorry!

3.5 stars.

I get that the chef wanted to have a ramen interpreted his way, but I just don't think it's as good. Perhaps, the flavors are on the bland side and the noodle texture is lacking. The food taste good and I believe the quality is good, but I can't warrant an extra star because I just prefer more traditional ramen. The service was also a little off-putting too...I would say snooty, which is a joke @ a ramen place.

Ambiance here was really cool but the ramen was very average. I went here w/ my friend Heather while visiting her in NYC. We were cold and searching for ramen to warm us up and this place was the closest. Kudos for great service though! :-)

Went for a quick lunch today. Being a ramen fan, I wasn't impressed with the shoyu ramen. The noodles are good but the broth needs depth. Something is definitely missing. It was also very very salty. I would try Ivan again when I have more time and can try more dishes. This is totally based on 1 ramen. The service was great!

Honestly my favorite ramen place in the city. I'd be here all the time if the Lower East Side were more accessible by train.

This is not for everyone--it's nothing like Ippudo, Totto, or Hide-chan, which I'm thankful for. There's less of a wait, and you won't feel overfull and greasy afterward. This is also fusion, but I don't think traditionalists will be disappointed. Whether you like Ivan Ramen will depend on whether you prefer: 1) thick or thin noodles (theirs are thin) and 2) fatty or light broth (theirs is mostly light, but pretty salty).

The atmosphere and staff are super hip, which I could take or leave, and it's slightly pricey, but the food is divine. I also recommend the drinks and desserts--they source special flavors from Dough. (I can never decide between Green Tea, Red Bean and Yuzu. Life is hard.)

Ivan Ramen was great! Came here for lunch on a warm afternoon and it proved to be the perfect time for two reasons:
1) No one was here and we didn't have a huge wait
2) They serve a cold ramen dish various other cold dishes/drinks

I wasn't blown away by the offerings but I still ate the whole meal. The cold ramen was unique and flavorful and the added egg was cooked to perfection. 

The lemonade was great but be warned that the cucumber version has lots of tiny green specs in it and I spent time picking them out of my teeth afterwards. Lots of little things to get stuck between teeth and gum lines.

The broth in the classic ramen is very dark and a little saltier than I am used to. I still liked it and the portion was massive. My fiancé and I split our two bowls to be able to try more dishes.

Service was fast and friendly. If I'm in the area I'd come back but it wasn't quite amazing enough to make a trip across town for. 

Make sure to check out the art on the walls. It's the story of how to eat ramen in a sort of Japanese graffiti style art. Very cool.

2 stars because my friends liked their meals.  I got the Tokyo Shiyu not fully loaded and for the price I was totally confused.  Chicken broth, 2 small slices of breast meat, scallions, noodles and an egg.  I could make it myself for a dollar.  Nice place, good service but way overpriced, even for NYC

*pork meatballs (I really liked the meatball itself, it was crispy on the outside the meat was sweet and juicy on the inside; that cream sauce on the plate was strange on its own but was decent when combined with the meat; definitely could handle only eating two of these)
*buckwheat waffles (pretty good!! I liked the waffles themselves, chewy in the middle with crisp edges; the ginger syrup was good and not overly sweet; the toasted soy whipped cream was not bad but they put WAY too much on the waffles!!! this was a doublestack of waffles and they put whipped cream in between as well which was not necessary. Since the waffles were warm, the cream melted anway and made the waffles more soggy than necessary in the middle. I think it would have been better to just keep the cream on top and just gave me the syrup on the side for the stack below)

This place is cute. I like the set up inside with the barstools and high tables and then the patio in the back. The food is decent. Not amazing. Would go back if invited with friends but not a place I'd personally choose.

Came here for dinner with my girls on a cold rainy November night aka perfect ramen weather. No wait and they seated me before the other 2 arrived which was nice. 

Very generous servings of ramen. The broth is flavorful and not too salty. Noodles are very well cooked and plentiful enough that you're not left with a lot of broth in the end. 

I wanted to sub my meat for egg or vegetable and that wasn't a problem but instead of a swap they charged me for the egg as an add on. The contents of the ramen are pretty basic so you can quickly get carried away with add ons so watch out!

We also got the deviled egg (Delish) and pork meatballs. I don't eat pork but my friends really liked them
I'm first time come to here . It's very delicious . The waiter is very friendly . I'm will come back next time . I think ivan ramen is best in Manhattan.

My first experience with Ivan Orkin's work was roughly a year ago, at the Gotham West Market location of Ivan Slurp Shop. I had been intrigued with the story - who wouldn't be? The success of a Jewish-American who moved to Japan with his wife and opened a successful ramen shop in the motherland isn't something that occurs every day. The bowl I had there, however, was one of the worst I can recall ever having [1], so I paid little attention to the fact that Orkin decided to open a proper brick-and-mortar in the Lower East Side. The menu here is notably different than the one found at Slurp Shop, but given my less-than-favorable first impression, I delayed a first visit until one of my ramen-obsessed friends persuaded me to join him here for dinner.

Unlike most ramen joints, Ivan Ramen accepts reservations online via OpenTable. While I'm not sure whether or not this is actually necessary, especially given the sheer volume of tables and seats available, it's an appreciated factor to those who want to negate the chance of lines or excessive wait times. On the warm evening we went, however, there were only a handful of other parties present, so we were given our pick of seats.

We started off with the Pork Meatballs, one of many of their unique appetizers. The meatballs are served 6 to an order, and served "takoyaki style" - topped with bulldog sauce, shaved bonito flakes... and Ivan's own buttermilk sauce (instead of the traditional kewpie mayonnaise). We were both delighted with this appetizer; the pork meatballs were crisp and firm on the outside like good takoyaki should be, but the interior was tender and piping hot. It's seasoned well, featuring a range of flavors across the spectrum of savory to sweet, and makes for a solid first bite.

We ordered two ramen bowls and split them; how could we not be tempted by the Spicy Red Chili Ramen or the Dan Dan Noodles? The first is one of the most iconic bowls at Ivan Ramen thanks to the sheer vibrant red hue of the broth, a sight that will deter the weak of heart. Spoiler: yes, it's pretty damn spicy. The base, Orkin's signature blend of half dashi and half chicken stock is intensified by the addition of doubanjang (a spicy red bean paste with origins from China) and copious amounts of chili oil. Add in a healthy serving of the chewy rye noodles, ground pork, and a smashed egg, and you have for yourself a dish that builds in spice, but not necessarily flavor, as you eat it; there wasn't much depth in the overly salted broth, and each spoonful became monotonous in taste the more we ate. For those with weaker stomachs: be warned of the aftereffects that will likely occur...

The Dan Dan Noodles, a riff on the popular Sichuan dish, was similarly a mixed bag. It's served "dry style", which means there's no actual broth within the bowl. Instead, the whole wheat noodles are coated in a sweet-savory sauce highlighted by sesame oil, and topped with a generous portion of ground pork, sesame seeds, and an egg yolk. As a firm loyalist to Han Dynasty's Dan Dan Mian, I will admit to an initial bias, but... these noodles are not as impressive. The sauce leans a little too much on the sweet side, and an additional punch of spice would have done wonders for the flavor profile. The noodles, however, were delightfully chewy and dense, and held up well while we went through the bowl. Also, for the carnivores, there's enough ground pork in the bowl to share with at least one or two other people.

While I find the execution of dishes to be notably better at Ivan Ramen (versus the Slurp Shop), the overall quality of the food is a mixed bag. The plates are unique and creative, yes, but I'd hazard to say that much of the focus on flavor and taste has been sacrificed in favor of sheer novelty. For the curious, it's certainly worth a visit, especially to try some of the appetizers (which seem to be better-received than the actual ramen); for the purists, however, never fear - NYC has plenty of excellent ramen shops just a stone's throw away.

A bit overrated and pricy, but fun place. Choice should definitely be bigger.. There are not that many ramen places on LES, it is good to have this one.

Ivan ramen is a quintessential example of NYC cuisine. There's definitely some interesting aspects of their menu and they manage to dazzle with the menu, but the food leaves something to be desired. 

They have the traditional shio as well as a spicy version of ramen also - all served with rye noodles. Noodle texture was great, I ordered it all the way: $5 extra for egg, and pork, but the flavor of the ramen leaves something to be desired. In the case of the spicy ramen, the spiciness was great but the broth wasn't correspondingly richer. Disappointing, there's plenty of potential with Ivan ramen's concept. 

Service was attentive, and the food was good - they need to step up their game to deliver the full ramen experience.

Ivan Ramen was different, in a good way though.  

We were running behind on our reservation, so I called to notify the hostesses. They were very pleasant and understanding. Even though we arrived after the grace period, they still held our table for us. 

To start we ordered the thousand year old deviled eggs and kyuri pickles. 

I was expecting an actual 1000 year old egg, instead the topping itself was a mixture of the 1000 year old egg topped with bonito flakes. However the menu does indeed state "hen egg + preserved duck egg, tomato, bonito". Guess I was too hungry to read!  This was delightful, it was strange to eat what looks like a regular egg with the taste of 1000 year old egg yolk. The taste of the 1000 year old egg yolk was not overpowering. 

The pickles were sweet and tangy. Despite the tastiness of these pickles it a little light on the portion for the price point. $7 - see photo.   

Like other reviewers have stated, the portions are a bit smaller at Ivan Ramen. However, I don't think that warrants a low rating, I left more than satisfied. 

I ordered the Spicy Red Chili Ramen, fully loaded. Don't forget to mix up the broth well as a lot of the spices is at the bottom of the bowl. I did no mix mine well enough and the broth at the end was very concentrated. 

Everything in the fully loaded add-ons are well worth the $5. The eggs were perfect, tender white egg and a silky creamy yolk, it was delicious eating together with the broth. A second piece of pork chashu would have been appreciated! :D The roasted tomatoes were nicely roasted and full of umami.

I know ramen comes in many different styles and forms, but this place was not for me. If you're looking to "expand" your ramen horizons then come here. If you're looking for traditional shoyu ramen, there are many other places I would go in NYC.

I think the best part of the meal was the spicy dill house-made pickles. I could eat those every day and be happy and the spice + herbs were a great counterpoint to the fatty, delicious ramen. Noon on a weekday, opentable reservation, but wasn't necessary at all, as there were two or three other people in the place. 

As everyone else has stated, pretty good, albeit a bit pricey ($12 for one bottle of beer? yea, it's a craft, but that's pretty up there).

I really don't understand what all the hate is about.
Ivan Ramen is different, and different is good. You don't come in here expecting your run of the mill shoyu ramen. Did you really expect that from someone whose name sounds like he's from Chernobyl but is actually from Long Island?
So far, I've tried the triple pork triple garlic mazemen, spicy red chili, tokyo shoyu, cold lemon shio ramen plus the tofu coney island. Out of everything I tried, only the tokyo shoyu was a miss (overly  salty, hence the four stars), but everything else was deliciously different. If you want to taste regular ramen, I'd suggest totto or hide-chan (but please not Ippudo, it's too...clean). But if you want New York's take on ramen, then I suggest you try out Ivan.

I loved this place!! Ramen was just great. It was late in the evening and the server brought extra small plates for tasting at n/c. All who work here are so charming and friendly. Can't wait to come back!
I would rate this is the best ramen on the lower east side!

Fully loaded spicy Chilly Ramen was incredible. The BEST Ramen ever!!
The service was good too. They have a tiny, cute outdoor area behind the restaurant, perfect for a weekend brunch.

Ivan has a modern-fusion take on ramen and some small dishes. They are a bit hit-and-miss, but it's worth checking out if you order the right things. Please see my photos for additional details/info!

RESERVATIONS: Easily made a few days in advance for a Monday night at 6:30pm. It wasn't too busy when we arrived.

THE COST: $26 total for my share of 2 starters and 3 noodle dishes, shared between three people.

MUST-HAVES: Tofu Coney Island for starters, Trip Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen for the ramen (universally agreed to at my table).

HOT
* Tofu Coney Island (miso mushroom chili, yellow mustard, scallion. $13) - 4 stars
This didn't sound too exciting to me (I thought it would be a tofu dog on a bun), but it's more like an Asian tofu dish with some new flavors. There was perfectly even breading on the tofu, and it came out to be a surprisingly great combination of flavors - I thought there was meat in the sauce! The crunchy fresh scallion to top it off was the cherry on top - a great addition.

HOUSE SPECIALTIES
* Braised Beef Tongue (dashi + beef broth, hot mustard. $15) - 3.5 stars
The meat was tender and really great, but it was way too salty. You definitely needed the mustard to counter it.

NOODLES
* Tokyo Shio Ramen (sea salts, dashi + chicken broth, pork chasu, egg, rye noodle. $15). 
I didn't try this, but my friend wasn't impressed and didn't finish his bowl.

* Spicy Red Chili Ramen (dashi + chicken broth, minced pork, smashed egg, rye noodle. $15) - 2.5 stars
I tried a bite and we all agreed; this was way too spicy, in a way that doesn't add flavor but is just painful. Our server did warn it would be really spicy, but a dish can definitely be this spicy and have more well-rounded flavors.

* Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen (tonkotsu broth, pork chat, whole wheat noodle. $16) - 4 stars
As our server described, this was more of a dry sauce noodle as opposed to being in a big bowl of broth, and this was exactly what I was in the mood for. The pork was delicious and the flavors were great - it was a tad on the salty side, but still everyone's favorite ramen by far.

Fully enjoyed dinner here the other night -- 3 diners, we were seated back in the corner banquette adjacent to the bar / garden door: comfortable and not cramped, with a good view of action in the restaurant. Our smiley waiter was enthusiastic, friendly and attentive.

We started with the pork meatballs with buttermilk dressing, bulldog sauce and bonito flakes. These incorporate whipped tofu and are very tender and light, with a crispy shell from frying -- delicious. The lemonades we ordered -- yuzu, Ivan Palmer & prickly pear -- were all very good.

For mains, we had the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen, the room-temp Tonkotsu Tsukemen, and the Iced Summer Shoyu with optional crab salad. All were excellent, relatively light on a midsummer's eve, flavor-packed and not overly salty at all. Obviously different from traditional ramen, but in a well-conceived, thoughtfully-balanced and tastily-executed way. Out choices provided good variety and contrast, from the chilled, vegetal, gazpacho-esque shoyu to the lift-and-dip noodles of the tsukemen, which also sported three cubes of warm fried pork belly and a semi-liquid half HB egg,

Reasonable tab / definitely would return.

The interior design and decor was really nice and caught my eye. Despite the aesthetically pleasing interior, the food was mediocre.

The old egg was very yummy, and gave us high expectations for the food, but the ramen failed to meet our expectations. The ramen was salty and somewhat difficult to enjoy.. Most likely won't be coming back.

Delicious. Split the daikon radish appetizer with a friend, and got the shoyu ramen (she got the shio bowl). The broth had so much depth and complexity, but was surprisingly *light* for such a hot summer day. Didn't weigh me down, and we both appreciated that the portion was a little smaller...ramen is so difficult to not finish, so we found ourselves pleasantly full at the end.

To pair with the heat, I got a freezing cold Hell or High Watermelon beer, which actually went super duper well with the hot, salty ramen. Great meal, friendly service, and nicely done decor. Can't wait to go back!
The bowl of ramen I had here was mediocre.  The pop art decor cheesy and kind of cold.

I'd heard a lot about this place and wanted to give it a try.  I was in the area one evening before a show and decided to try it by myself.  I had no trouble getting in although I was probably there on the earlier side.  They seated me at the counter and the waiter was very nice to me.  The decor was interesting but unfortunately the food just wasn't that good, particularly for the price.  I've had a fair amount of ramen in my time and I found there to be nothing special about this.  In fact it was a little too salty for my taste.  Overall I just wasn't that satisfied.  I tried it and so now it's off my list but it's not a place I would ever take anyone to should they visit NYC or recommend to a friend.
This place came highly recommended to me but I left very disappointed.  So many better ramen pls end on Manhattan to try!

It's the summer. It's that time of year when the oven is off-limits, and my diet consists of ice cream, water, fruit, and hiyashi chuka. 

When I heard that Chef Ivan Orkin created a series of cold ramen dishes (hiyashi chuka, a cold shio ramen, a cold shoyu ramen, AND a tonkotsu tsukemen), I knew I had to try as many as possible. Gotta catch 'em all, you know?

Hiyashi chuka is a type of summer dish typically served on a flat plate that contains cold ramen noodles dressed in a soy sauce or miso dressing, with lots of vegetables on top. The version at Ivan Ramen is lovely. 

Here are some bullet points because it's a lazy summer day:

 - it's served with springy, whole wheat, thick ramen noodles (I'm not a fan of his rye noodles)
 - it's not drenched in his honey soy sauce dashi dressing and the dressing itself is refreshing and vinegary
 - the toppings are really crunchy and plentiful: there are cucumbers, tomatoes, ham, lettuce, eggs, daikon, bacon bits, and nori
 - he really knows how to work different textures and flavors; there's umami, salt, sweet, sour, and bitter all satisfyingly contained in one dish

The tonkotsu tsukemen, cold rye noodles with a lukewarm broth for dipping, was just okay. The broth was way too rich and fatty for my taste. 

I still stand by the roast pork musubi as being one of the finest appetizers. 
 

Likelihood of another visit:
They take reservations now! If you're going to be here on a weekend night around 8pm, it might be better to look on Opentable just in case. As for the other cold ramen dishes that are just like the hot ramen, but with ice cold soups, I'm curious, but not curious enough to stray from the delightful hiyashi chuka I had. I'll be back this summer.
I still crave their Ramen. It's a little cramped but not too much so for extra noodles all around! Yum.

It has an interesting twist to the traditional Japanese ramen. Aside from soy base and miso base soups they also have exotic flavored based soups. Some of the toppings were new and exciting for pairing but not all of them worked with the dish. The roast pork could've been a bit more tender, but otherwise this place is worth a try.

Many people told me about this place so I decided to try it out.
Its one of those places that you would try once, know what its about so you dont feel left out when people talk about it, but will never go back.
Food was mediocre and service was not up to par.

An acquaintance highly recommended Ivan ramen even going in so far to say that it was the best ramen he had ever had. So as you can guess, I went in with high expectations. 

The staff at Ivan Ramen are great! Our bartender/ waiter was super friendly. A+ for them. Decor was pretty neat.

I kicked of my night with a "Yuzu Lemonade" and "Mushroom Casino" for my appetizer. You can't really mess up lemonade, so that's that. As for the mushroom casino, that was something really unique. It consisted of SUPER THIN slices of mushroom (achieved using a deli slicer) mixed with baby clams and covered in panko (Japanese bread crumbs). It tasted good, but unfortunately I found it very heavy for an appetizer. It killed my appetite almost instantly. But alas I needed to push on and try something from the noodle menu. 

Due to it being a hot muggy summer day, I decided to go with the Tonkotsu Tsukemen (cold noodles with pork based dipping sauce). This was one of the oiliest things I have ever consumed in my life! The noodles were so slick, I'm sure they were dipped in oil, and the dipping broth was pretty much straight up pig fat. Also included were three cubes of fried fatty pork to top it off. I was wiping the oil off my lips after every bite. I tried to spice up the flavor by adding some panko, cilantro, and chili to it, but the concentration of bland pork fat was just too much. 

After eating my tsukemen, I had the opportunity to taste the "Triple Garlic Ramen." The broth was just as fatty and thick as the tsukemen! No salvation was found whatsoever in this dish.

I have no idea how many people find Ivan ramen's broth flavorful and unique. It was just bland, thick, and oily. I would only recommend you come here if you really love your animal fat, or if you are a car in need of an oil change.

I first tried Ivan Orkin's ramen in his Tokyo locations and I really enjoyed it, so I was glad to see that he opened a location in New York. At this location, I tried the summer special, which was the cold noodle tonkotsu tsukemen (dipping style ramen). It was quite refreshing to eat during the hot and humid summer season, especially because the tonkotsu was not as heavy as the average tonkotsu soup. My slight disappointment was that the soft boiled egg was not seasoned.

I appreciate and enjoy Ivan's own take on ramen. His version seems cleaner and more refined than what you would traditionally get. Don't get me wrong, I love all types and styles of ramen. I like to think of this as another regional style of ramen.

I think the Yelp reviews are pretty spot on.  This place is a 3.5 stars for me.  It is a solid 4 for food and service, but take away 1/2 a star for value.

My daughter and I stopped for lunch while on vacation.  I had read about his story and have seen a few clips on TV so it intrigued me.  I mean this Jewish guy from NY was very popular in Tokyo right?  Upon arrival, the storefront is very unassuming.  There is a small dining area which leads to a longish corridor that opens up to the kitchen/counter, more dining space and a small patio.  Everything is clean and modern.

We were greeted immediately by both our server and the manager.  Everyone was courteous and helpful.  We started with some roast pork musubi.  These were pretty tasty, but not musubi in the true sense, more like nigiri sushi intended to be consumed in one bite.  Next we had the pork meatballs.  They had a nice crispy outside to contrast to the tender meat in the middle.  Topped with katsu sauce, buttermilk dressing and katsuo boshi, they were delicious.  Lastly, we shared a shoyu ramen.  I was a little disappointed because I wanted to taste the shio ramen he is famous for, but it's not on the lunch menu.  In fact, my second choice would have been the triple pork, triple garlic mazemen, but that too is absent during lunch.  In any case, the ramen was good.  The broth definitely highlighted the soy sauce flavor without being overly salty.  The rye noodles are different and add another nice layer of flavor.

In the end, it was a cool experience and I'm glad I tried it, but it's definitely more of a destination place for me.  All in, our bill was about $65 and we shared a bowl of ramen.  I don't know how the ramen in NYC is, but I'm guessing that there are at least a handful of great places.  I know that in LA, you can grab a top notch bowl of ramen (sans rye noodles) for much much less.

Was pleasantly surprised how delicious it was. I was a little hesitant because it was considered fusion and I LOVE the full on Japanese ramen. Gave the Triple Pork ramen a try with the rye noodles and was not disappointed! I did kaedama afterwards and they gave me the whole wheat ramen noodles and that was really delicious as well. Definitely would come back.

For the normal ramen, flavor is lacking. 

Cold ramen was really refreshing but it felt like something was missing.

The hostesses were pretty pretentious. Walked in to a pretty empty restaurant and they immediately asked us with a raised eyebrow and attitude if we had a reservation... They seemed kind of reluctant to seat us... in the empty restaurant. 

+ Waiter keeps your water full 
+ Space outside is nice

Went in for a weekday lunch on a hot and humid day so it was great to see a few cold dish options available.  They just opened when we arrived and the place was pretty quiet while we were there with 2 or 3 other parties.  Rundown of what we had:

Roast Pork Musubi:  Wish the portion was bigger.  Felt like I was having an amuse bouche with an almost one bite portion.  The flavor was fine but I don't remember tasting the salted plum.  Didn't knock my socks off.

Iced Summer Shoyu Ramen: never thought about having cold ramen and this was a great option to beat the heat.  No meat included unless you add on crab, but I don't think this dish really needs it.  For a light, summer dish, the vegetables and noodles were just right.  The dashi & ponzu soup was nice and chilled.  Really delicous and provided the umami flavor to round out the dish.  The soup had a great balance of salty and a little tartness.  Very pleased with this cold soup.

Tonkatsu Tsukemen:  Mazemen was not offered on the lunch menu so ordered this dish instead.  The rye noodles are chilled and had a nice bouncy bite to them.  The tonkatsu broth is served in the side for dipping the noodles.  The broth is a very rich, concentrated pork flavor with a gravy consistency than a broth.  It coats the noodles and the tongue nicely and you don't need a lot.  The broth has little bits of pork, and three fried cubes of pork & half of a soft boiled egg come on top of the noodles.  Thought I may run out of broth, but I was impressed in the end that just the right amount of broth was served for the amount of noodles. There's the option to add on more pork, but I didn't need it. 

Hope to go back to try the mazemen and hot ramen when the weather is cooler.

We had the spicy red chili ramen - fully loaded. It was really good, spicy but not too spicy. The eggs were wonderful. The tomato was a great surprise, went really well with the rest of the flavors. I had to take 2 stars away because midway through eating the bowl, the broth was horrendously salty and we couldn't finish the remaining bowl. This was a shame because we still had noodles and pork. At $20 for the bowl, we wanted to finish it all.

After walking around New York's Chinatown all day, I was surprised at how happy I was to happen upon this ramen place for dinner. You'd think that knowing that we had probably walked by and missed an authentic  unassuming noodle place where an old man was labouring in the basement pulling the noodles by hand would diminish our satisfaction... But it didn't.
First of all here's our order:
Beef Tongue - I've officially fallen in love with hot beef tongue. In my family we eat it sliced thin cold on a plate, but I'd push that aside for this warm cubed deliciousness. It was surprisingly tender and flavorful and the broth that came poured over it was sweet salty and scrumptious. Don't miss out on the yellow dipping sauce on the side, it looks like mustard but tastes like its got wasabi mixed into it.
Spicy Red Chili Ramen - the boy got the spicy ramen, of course. We both really love spice and he has pretty high standards for his spicy noodles. I had a bite, it was quite yummy but not as spicy as you'd think.
Tokyo Shoyu Ramen - the dish I got since I wasnt going to get the same ramen as he did (madness, why order the same thing when you can order different things and trade) which was very yummy. The soup was nice and salty and the noodles had a good texture to them. Yum for soft boiled eggs and charsiu.
The place is great. Tiny, but great. It has a bar you can eat at alone if you feel the craving and don't have a noodle buddy.
We drank beer with bulldog sauce in it, I can't remember the name, but it was quite the yummy cocktail for a sunday night where we weren't feeling the hard liquor scene.
It also has an outside patio dining area which I would definitely try for next time.
Random noodle bar happiness.

*Disclaimer we were pretty much starving. This review is definitely biased.

I have been to Ivan Ramen twice and I think I would visit again soon. I tried the Tokyo Shio Ramen and the Cold Lemon Shio Ramen. Both were very good. I like the dashi broth as part of base the soup. All flavors comes together and suits each other well. The rye noodle is special and good, too. The ramen is on the expensive side but I think it worths the price. I would recommend it over Ippudo, and I think it can compete with Totto Ramen and Mu Ramen. Another place to consider in LES on Sunday evening is Benkei Ramen at Hill & Dale.

If you want a no-frills, high quality ramen experience, this is the place for you. 

I had the Tokyo Shio ramen, which replaces sea salt for soy sauce, and it was one of the tastiest bowls I've had in awhile. The noodles were divine and the broth perfectly eliminated my hangover from the night before. 

It's a good place for solo dining, though I'd like to come back with a friend so I can try as much food as possible. Thank goodness they take reservations!

Wow..lots of very long reviews! My first Ramen experience was a good one! The triple pork ramen..fully loaded is the way to go. The noodles, chewy ,in the best possible way! The hearty broth was more of a sauce. The pork so tender. All in all, a great experience. The wait staff was very informative. Great quirky decor. My only minus...the cost of the 6 meaty yet small ribs. Though spicey with a great chew, they were $21.00. This will be what all other Ramen will be compared to. We ll be back!
Love this place. The spicy red ramen is my fav. It's a staple for me in my line up of go to restaurants.

Lovely atmosphere but I have to give it 3 stars because:
- way too overpriced
- hardly any gluten-free or vegetarian options. Almost all of the broth is made with pork and the noodles are made with rye
- did I mention how overpriced this ramen is?
- the broth was hella salty and undiluted

Food hasn't even come out yet and I already vote ippudo the better restaurant. Who's bright idea was to serve ramen in an open patio when it's 80 degrees outside and humid. Keep the top closed and blast the AC. Morons. 2 stars for dumb planning. It would've been one star if the appetizers sucked but it's ok. We'll see if they maintain the stars when the ramen (without broth because they don't do that by the way) comes out. 

Update. Messed up order.

This place must be making a killing charging $15 for such meager food. They even skimped out on broth. I got one slice of pork with my ramen. I did however get a lot of noodles so that I felt like I was eating a pasta dish more than anything. My boyfriend got the soy based broth and that is all it tasted like. On the positive side the hard boiled egg was really good.

I liked the food and vibe here. You can sit alone at the bar or have a casual lunch with friends. I like that you can see people making your food. It's on the pricier side for Ramen (paying for ambiance). My only real complaints are the lack of free refills on the barley tea (its $3 and it's tea!) and that they don't do takeout as of writing this.
I could eat nothing but the spicy chili ramen for the rest of my life. It's that good. The sweet potato dish is great too but wicked overpriced ($7 for a few slivers of sweet potato? C'mon.)

5 other people with me on the patio, and we had a great time! I had an order of the L.E.S. Buns and the Triple Pork Mazemen, both were outstanding. Beer selection was great, service was great. Overall....you guessed it...great! Well done Ivan.

Decor's cool, with its graffitied up walls.

Located in LES, Ivan Ramen doesn't deliver to the NYC ramen scene. Tried both their Tokyo Shio ramen and their Spicy Chili Oil Ramen, and the broth was too salty and single-dimensional. Go somewhere else, there's tons of better ramen shops in the city.

Kool ambiance and really good service.  But in terms of value compared to other many good ramen shops in NYC this is just OK for me.  Value wise, portions are smaller and prices are def on higher end even for NYC.  No doubt the ramen is delicious but I'd say on par with other top ramen spots in the city.  Id say the broth here is extremely flavorful but they dont give enough fillings or noodles in the ramen for me.  If you come hungry you'll need appz and dessert.

Overall def worth checking out for sure, def a a trendy scene.  But expect to drop some $$.

Came for lunch and was disappointed that three things I really wanted to order were not offered on the lunch menu (ankimo dirty rice, triple pork/triple garlic mazemen and the four cheese mazemen).

So we ordered:
- pork meatballs - liked the meatballs but did not like the sauce that were drizzled on them.... should have asked for the sauce on the side since we felt it overpowered the meatballs
- fully loaded ramen- good but nothing special
- cold lemon shio ramen- enjoyed these refreshing noodles and would have never ordered it had the server not suggested it... glad she did
- spicy red chili ramen- these were good but again, not outstanding

We plan to return for dinner to try what we were determined to originally try... Ivan Ramen... you should really put those three dishes on your lunch menu.

This place is so tasty! The menu is very interesting, with a lot of great twists to a classic taste. The serving size is perfect -- not too much food, and not too little, either. The only problem is it seems a little expensive for what you are getting. The ambiance is trendy and fun. The service is prompt and good.

My roommate told me about this place. Since i love ramen and even made it from scratch before i was interested to see an american take on japanese ramen. Holy hell it was such a major disappointment. The food was good to okay. Nothing great that distinguish this place to momofoku or other high end ramen places. The noodles werent even hand made. The prices are stupid high for what you get. Try it once and avoid

Mediocre. Would've given three stars but the price is high compared to other better and cheaper options in NYC (e.g. Tabata in Hell's Kitchen). 

I tried the Triple Pork and Spicy ramen.

The apps and ramen were fantastic. Get the mushrooms casino. Triple pork/triple garlic was super decadent but not too large of a serving, so you're satisfied without feeling stuffed. The meal was too expensive, however. $100 (not incl tip) for 2 apps, 2 bowls of ramen, and a shared 300ml modestly priced bottle of sake. Ramen dinners shouldn't cost that much.

Good noodles, well-cooked egg and yummy pork. However the Tokyo shoyu broth is WAY salty for my taste so this would be one of my least favorite "famous" my ramen spots. Also had a cold daikon appetizer and the flavors weren't super balanced on that either. Not bad, but not my style.

Note -I accidentally had called the Tokyo shoyu broth "miso" broth in my earlier review.

The noodles was not super salty but it was probably because i didn't drink the soup. and there as like 2 pieces of meat. It definitely not worth the price and I left feeling hungry. My friends had the spicy ramen and they have pretty good spice tolerance so they thought the noodles wasn't too spicy. We had a back picnic table all to ourselves with glass covering. it was very nice and peaceful. I liked the atmosphere but the food is way too expensive. I am not a big ramen person so I didn't think the noodles were that awesome.
Sucked!  Will never go again.  Ramen portions were small and needed to get a slice of pizza afterwards.  Ramen is over priced.  Not worth it. Don't waste your time or $$$.  Sorry Ivan!
Soooo good. Staff is always friendly and informative, food is absolutely delicious. Every appetizer is amazing.

Ivan Ramen was the first of its kind that I've tried since I was used to the flavors of Ippudo and Totto. My first visit was actually in the one at Gotham West Market, so I was pleased that I didn't have to travel too far for this one on Clinton St. I'm assuming the low ratings for this place is for people who aren't too used to this style of ramen or they're not too happy with the service. I, for one, am very fond of the Shoyu Ramen for its simplicity. But for service, I was really taken back by one of the managers I'm assuming that was there and her attitude towards the other employees. She made the atmosphere tense and uncomfortable even for a customer eating at the bar. I hope they really don't rely on these kind of people to manage a restaurant.

In the search of top-quality ramen in NYC, Ivan Ramen falls in perhaps the top 10. Not a must, but they've got some solid offerings besides ramen that I think are even better! 

Their roast pork Musubi is as tasty as it is pricey for the quantity. Roasted tomato and pork have never had such a delicious pairing! I also highly recommend the mushroom casino. Flavorful, crunchy, and topped with savory bits of clam and sausage. This was the favorite of the table. The tempura ebi would have been good I'm sure, that is--if we didn't have to split two shrimps between five people. The watercress salad underneath had a deep, herby flavor--not for everyone. 

The ramen itself I found to be rather unique though slightly disappointing. I enjoyed the smoky flavor of the broth and noodles, but the entirety of the dish was lacking. A slice of pork that was 90% fat (of course it's delicious but it's difficult to mess up a slice of pork fat.) An egg, strips of scallion...and yep, that's it. Not much of a bowl of ramen I'm afraid. I can't say I'm dying to go back, but try it for yourself and see what you think!
Great service! The side dishes are delish the ramen is good but not amazing I have had amazing. Though the pork belly is very tender very good pork!

I love ramen and with a recent gluten allergy plaguing my body, I was really excited to try this place as I saw they offered gluten-free tofu noodles and a ton of veggie options. When beginning to order, I was really disappointed to hear that most of their broths are made of real soy sauce (which contains a large amount of wheat). I wish they were more explicit about allergens on the menu. The server, however, asked right when we sat down about any food allergies and was helpful in explaining how foods were prepared. Too little, too late, though. My guest ordered a snack, the L.E.S buns (just a greasy mess), until we could head somewhere else for a meal. A great unfiltered sake was the silver lining.
it's more like a fusion ramen, even more inclined to chinese than japanese I'd say, the noodle/soup and the appetizers we had all tasted similar at home (and unfortunately in a bad way, very linear)

So I have to admit with some astonishment that I was marginally disappointed with this place, and I am not as much of a ramen connoisseur as others are, including presumably owner Ivan Orkin, a New York native who developed major cred by opening up two popular ramen houses in Tokyo. He opened two more shops in Manhattan, wrote a ramen cookbook, and is an FOD - friend of David, Chang that is, since he's featured often in Chang's foodie magazine, Lucky Peach. I don't doubt that Ivan knows noodles, but the lack of a true Tonkotsu Ramen choice on the menu disturbed me.

I don't count the $16 Tonkotsu Tsukemen, which provides cold wheat noodles to dip into a tonkotsu broth. In fact, I'm miffed they would go to the trouble of making tsukemen and not use the same broth for a classic ramen bowl. Ivan is not alone in his thinking. Michael Mina made the same mistake to exclude it from his Ramen Bar, and writing on behalf of the many tonkotsu fans out there, we are not happy. Regardless, I distracted myself by ordering the $7 Roast Pork Musubi, a pair of wing-tipped nori toasted with salted plum wasabi, roasted tomato, rice and bits of pulled pork (photo: http://bit.ly/1LnTuID). Tasty morsels, they were easy to pop in the mouth and gone in a matter of seconds.

But then came the tonkotsu-less ramen decision, and I chose the $15 Tokyo Shoyu Ramen simply because I presumed the Shio version would be more watered down. I was underwhelmed by the thin chicken broth that was blended with soy sauce and dashi. I ordered extra pork belly for $3 more, and that helped fortify the bowl as did the semi-soft-boiled egg. The rye noodles not so much as I would have preferred regular noodles al dente instead (photo: http://bit.ly/1ReaVi9). I also found the service a bit on the lax side as the server did not appear genuinely concerned about my reaction to the lack of tonkotsu ramen.

On the upside, the shop is surprisingly spacious for a ramen operation, which is usually a study in claustrophobia. The main dining wall is a colorful decoupage of mostly Japanese pop and commercial art images (photo: http://bit.ly/1ZHBmTx). The restroom even has a framed poster of Woody Allen's "Manhattan" with Japanese subtitles. All these touches along with the urban-chic Lower East Side location provided the requisite coolness factor they were striving for, but all this plebeian wanted was a bowl of tonkotsu ramen to slurp up with abandon. It just didn't happen for me here.

FOOD - 3 stars...creative musubi but the watery ramen broth didn't satisfy
AMBIANCE - 3.5 stars...more spacious and less crowded than I was expecting
SERVICE - 2.5 stars...lackadaisical
TOTAL - 3 stars...the hype pushed my expectations too high for this shop

I stopped in for lunch during the week.  Though this is obviously a very good ramen place, I was in the mood for a sandwich. They have a ridiculously sloppy and delicious one called the Herbie's International, inspired by the old school Catskills sandwiches.  The flavors are to die for and it's literally finger-licking good.  Highly recommend.  Oh yeah and the staff was super nice to me and my young daughter.  Kudos!
I don't get the hype. I went in with very high expectations and left feeling disappointed. Ramen was beyond salty and way overpriced for the amount of food you get. Try Ippudo instead.

I lived in Tokyo for six years so I am literally always in the mood for ramen.  I went to check this place out for lunch with some friends.  It was chilly, but we sat outside with the heaters on because the place was packed--honestly not the best experience, unfortunately. With the heaters on it was too hot and with them off, pretty chilly.  We settled for off.  The Ichiban was 8 bucks--(again, I'm from NOT NYC so I'm not used to these prices) and they should have some Asahi Super Dry!

The ramen was poor at best--I hate to say it!  15 dollars for some of the blandest ramen I've had in a while.  There was no substance, unfortunately.  I was surprised that my meal literally consisted of broth, some arugula, mushrooms and two sundried tomatoes(?).  Nothing else.  Really, I'd say pop by if you're in the neighborhood and famished.  You might need to buy two ramen bowls.

My son is a foodie and studies up on chefs and restaurants and suggested this restaurant. So when I was making a trip to New York with my daughters we had to make a trip here. We were not disappointed. We were fortunate to have good weather and sat in the back. It all felt so perfect. The waiter was very helpful with explaining the menu. It is one of my top memories in New York. It really surprised me. I thought, really - a restaurant for noodles? But it was great. We loved everything we ate. 

We started the meal with the pickled Daikon and the pork meatballs. They were both amazing. I had the spicy red chili Ramen and loved it. I love hot spicy food and this was great. 
It is always great when the food and surroundings are both great. Such a wonderful memory. The only negative is that I have found is that they are just too far from California!

after the 3 stars slurp-shop in the far west i was expecting something similar... but surprise surprise the Tonkotsu Tsukemen here is orgasmic, every piece of it starting with the broth.
i have a 3 level canon to judge ramen: 1st the ramen i spit on it. 2nd the ramen was good but i don t dream about to get it again. 3rd the ramen that comes to my mind while having an orgasm. well, this was a #3. service & ambience...good.

Hmmm yeah this is was my second dinner of the night.  The spicy ramen was good and the special fried oyster was divine, however the triple pork ramen was very disappointing.  The nice waiter warned us about the ramen being very heavy and broth is thick, but still didn't prepare us for it.  This really should be a 3.5, but again: I had 1st dinner only 2 hours prior...

Love coming here for a cheap dinner in LES.  Nice cheffy take on ramen cuisine.  Their apps are always interesting.  Beef tongue, pastrami buns, kewpie ebi... seriously all their apps are awesome! Try the funky ones.  Only wish their ramen add on's included bamboo shoots.

I would first like to start by saying that this is an amazing place. When we first arrived the host told us it would be an hour and a half wait. We left and then I decided to check on line if I was able to get a reservation. I was. Within 15 mins! Went back in and told her we had reservations and were immediately seated. Service was ok. Food was great and very well prepared. However the pork noodle I ordered lacked the broth so the noodles were dry and sticky. Over all it was a good experience.

I ordered the following which composed up the lunch express.  It's honestly one of the best meals, minus drinks.  Not too bad if you compared price to price on the individual items off the menu:

Tokyo Shoyu (soy sauce) ramen
Pickled Daikon appetizer
Yuzu lemonade

--------

Pickled Daikon: this was by far one of my most favorite appetizers that I have eaten.  Pickled daikon is a very common appetizer but the topping that was used is very unique to SE Asia.  Boasting a flavor very similar to the fermented shrimp paste, belacan (blah-chan), the roasted bits are added on top.

PROS
-amazing combination of flavor: the roasted topping shrimp bits really complemented the tang of the vinegar
-not overly sour, not overly sweet: great balance
-good quantity: I definitely had enough to munch on and still save some for the ramen.  In fact, it was almost hard to finish!

CONS
-none really.  I could have used more of the shrimp paste topping though.

--------

Tokyo Shoyu Ramen:  I always forget that shoyu is essentially just soy sauce.  However, it seemed to be right up there in popularity after tonkatsu ramen so I figured it was worth trying.

PROS
-great quantity, not skimpy on the toppings or the noodles
-already comes with egg: I added the extras which included grilled tomatoes and egg so I essentially had two eggs with my ramen.
-Chasu was not overly dried.  It wasn't the best but I've had worse pieces of meat in ramen.

CONS
-salty.  I guess that's what happens when you order a soy-sauce ramen which by itself it is already salty in nature.
-I don't think the ramen noodles were that great.  They weren't as chewy as I prefer them but they weren't all that bad in and of itself.

--------

Yuzu Lemonade:  I loved this drink.  I love yuzu in general.  A fruit local to Japan, it's difficult to find in the US.  The taste is similar to that of a grapefruit from what my Japanese friends have told me, but yet it's not as bitter.  Yuzu aroma is also something very pleasant, something that really rejuvenates me.  They have an Ivan Palmer which is essentially a Yuzu lemonade with pomegranate juice.  I think I'll have to try that next time.

PROS
-good flavor: not overly sour but not overly sweet either.
-very refreshing, definitely cleanses the palate.

CONS
-none.


I'd totally go back for the pickled daikon and possibly to try a few other things on the menu.  I can't say it was crazy impressive, but that yuzu lemonade is really addicting!  Pictures here, similar post though so you can skip all that: https://rammiegirl.wordpress.com/2015/11/09/an-atlantan-in-new-york-rock-n-roll-brooklyn-half-part-6/

do not go there!!! this is the one of the worst ramen restaurant in new york!!! their broth tasts very instant and the noodle is so over-boiled. the waitress is too bossy to tell me how to eat noodle even though i am japanese!!! i can't believe people still talk about this restaurant and go eat. stop going there!!! their ramen is not a real ramen. period.

Ivan ramen was good. Not the best I've ever had but since most ramen places don't take reservation it is a little easier to come here. Also the backyard is cute and good for larger groups. 

I was really hoping they had some kind of non-pork buns (ippudo has veggie, momofuku has veggie or shrimp) so I was pretty disappointed to find out they didn't.

We ordered cucumber pickles ($7) to start which were good but kind of pricy. I got the vegetable ramen and asked for a side of spicy sauce. The ramen was alright. It had enoki mushrooms, tomato and arugula. I added an egg for another $2 which brought the ramen to $17. I felt like for that price it wasn't really worth it. I find The veggie ramen at ippudo much better, mostly because it comes with a lot more stuff in it and is larger. 

Will I be back? Probably if I have to wait 3 hours elsewhere for ramen but it wouldn't be my first choice.
The ramen and the Rye noodles were delicious, broth a little bit salty . Love the pastrami buns but It would be a nice addition vegetarian buns to the menu. Definitely I'll come back

Let me start by saying that I came across this place in Time Out's best ramen places in New York list where it was rated #2! Can't really judge ramen there cause I'm not a big fan and neither a ramen expert, however I had an expert by my side and she was not impressed. It was OK. Other than that, the place looks cool, nice design, clean, and staff was friendly.

Heard about this through one of my friends, and decided to come here on a whim. It sounded like this place gets packed easily, so we decided to make a reservation.

My boyfriend called in to make the reservation for 6:30PM on 11/19, and to ensure that our reservation was there, I also made a reservation on OpenTable for the same time (a picture attached as proof).

To our confusion, neither of our reservations showed up in their system....what???

But no worries, says the hostess - she seats us anyway; thankfully, because there were a few opened tables, and I would've been pretty upset, considering I had a confirmation!

Bussers are pretty quick to fill our glasses with water, and shortly after, a waitress came by to check on us, but we weren't ready yet. She did tell us about their special, which was the Japanese fried oysters, and then left us to decide what we wanted.

When we were ready, no waiters were around, so we flagged down the hostess nearby us. Pro-tip: The hostesses are literally there for that reason - to host - they don't take orders, or refill glasses, so don't expect them to assist you like your waiters would. She helped us get a waiter to come take down our order.

We ordered the special fried oysters, the spicy ramen (fully loaded, plus mushrooms),  and the shoyu ramen (plus mushrooms, and additional pork chashu). 

The oysters came out first, and the waitress explained that the sauce goes well with almost anything, and left us to our food. The oysters were juicy on the inside, even after being fried, and the sauce definitely made it taste great. I liked the cabbage slaw, also with the sauce, LOL.

We were left waiting for our ramen, but no matter - we didn't mind.
When it did come though, the first thing we noticed is that the spicy ramen didn't come with the mushrooms, as ordered. We called the waitress over and let her know, and she just brought the mushrooms over without question.

In terms of the Shoyu Ramen, the noodles, I liked the texture. In terms of taste, it didn't *wow* me, but it definitely was not terrible. Maybe the hype of it being "really good" killed it for me. The texture of the pork chashu was close to what I expected: soft, and flakes apart when bit. HOWEVER, the taste was subpar - I had ordered extra, so I received 3 pieces. I ate 2, but I couldn't stomach the last piece at all. There was something about the taste that didn't mix well with the ramen/soup. The color was a little off from what I'm used to (it was like greyish brown?? - wish I took a picture of it), but I don't know if that had something to do with the taste...

In terms of the spicy ramen, it was relatively spicy, but you won't die (for those who are sensitive to spicy foods). Since my boyfriend ate this, he enjoyed it, but wished there was more in portion. He ate my last piece of chashu, and agreed that there was something off about the taste.

I think overall, I was disappointed with my experience, but I might come back with the friend who recommended that I try this place out. Hopefully my experience will change for the better?? The staff was relatively friendly.

For the record, it did annoy me that our reservations didn't show up on the OpenTable or the phone call we made - like who answered the call, and why wasn't it there? Weird.

Totally trekked out here alone one night after a bunch of meetings and it was a nice hearty meal. I had the Mazemen noodles and it was really delicious, but I wish they mentioned that tiny dried shrimp was also added to the dish. Just slightly allergic and if I knew that it had that particular ingredient I would have chosen something else. It did give the overall taste a nice salty flavoring. Downed the meal with a beer and it was perfect pairing.

Interesting take on Ramen.  Located in the heart of LES, and with a Russian/Jewish chef, Ivan Ramen adds those influences to some really great ramen.  The most successful was the LES (pastrami) buns.

We ate outside on the patio - a really lovely space with interesting mural on the surrounding wall. Service was slow but professional, the inside space was pretty crowded and I think we got a little less attention out back.

Came here around 9pm on a Mon evening and it was a full house. Only had to wait 10 mins for a table to clear. Ordered the triple pork, triple garlic ramen plus an egg which has less broth and is meant to mix in with the wavy noodles for a thicker consistency. It included one extremely fatty slice of pork belly that I had a tiny bite of and what appeared to be bacon which made the ramen very salty. No idea what and where the third type of pork was.  Dish was okay, would not order again. Friend ordered the tokyo shoyu ramen. I liked this one better as it is more typical of conventional ramen and has a soy sauce soup base. I enjoyed the thin straight noodles but again the dish was overall a tad too salty. I will prob venture to another ramen place before coming here again.

I love me some ramen, but to be honest the only thing that I remember from my last meal at Ivan was the LES bun appetizer, which I would have never ordered if the server hadn't suggested it. It's two steamed buns with pastrami, karashi mayo, and daikon slaw. It sounds like a weird combo but it's so delicious - definitely don't miss it! 

As far as the ramen goes, I know I had something chilled but I can't for the life of me remember anything about the flavor or ingredients except that it was underwhelming. And when it comes to food I'm practically at Rain Main status so it's saying a lot that I can't recall anything special about it at all. 

It was a nice cool treat on a warm day, though, and at late brunch time on a Sunday it was pretty empty. The space is fun and whimsically decorated, and our server was above-and-beyond nice and friendly. For those reasons and mostly for the buns, I'd definitely return to give it another shot, but I wasn't bowled over by my Ivan experience.

The outdoor patio space is pretty cool, but the ramen was somewhere between mediocre and slightly disappointing. We got here at 2pm on a Sunday and it was pretty busy -- only seats at the bar were available right away. I ordered the spicy ramen. The ramen usually comes with minced pork, and I asked our waiter to substitute to the chasu, but he informed me that they don't do substitutions. I decided to cough up to $3 to add it to my dish. The spicy ramen was.. spicy but there was a lot of grittiness to the broth that I didn't like. I wouldn't go back on my own accord, but if we were in LES and someone wanted to grab ramen, I wouldn't be that sad to come back.

I had the Shio Ramen. I can see why the rye noodles are talked about -- they are soft, thin, and don't feel so heavy. The chicken and dashi broth is interesting but a little too much dashi for my taste. I think the seawood in the Shio Ramen is weird and there is not much meat (but the meat is good).

My wife had the Mazemen and that was delicious.

What stood out were the appetizers.  We had the Chinese broccoli (had a really nicely flavored sauce), beef tongue (very tender), and Coney Island tofu (their play on chili cheese hot dogs -- interesting and tasty!).
the garlic mazemen is, of course, delicious.  the spicy noodles are also delicious.  would happily come back.

I gave IR four stars because I appreciate its presence/creativity/innovation in the NY ramen scene. I tried to be open-minded and judge each item as its own unique statement as oppose to "what traditional ramen/Japanese cuisine is suppose to be". 

That said, we order the shio as well as the tsukemen. Again as its "own thing", it was good, but for my taste preference, I prefer the typical Japanese ramen. The tsukemen was pretty delicious, though I would have preferred more toppings with the standard order (for $16, the price seemed a bit steep for what was given).

I appreciate its narrative in the ramen craze here in NY, but would prefer just to go to Setagaya (again, just for my taste preference/budget!)

If you do decide to go, from what I have tried, I would recommend the tsukemen with extra toppings.

Such a shame. I REALLY wanted to like/ LOVE Ivan Ramen I just couldn't. I have read the other reviews on here for Ivan and I wonder if the people who love it just don't know any better. That is the only way I can justify it in my mind. I went to Ivan once earlier this year and thought it was just ok- not bad not good. I was a little tipsy so I figured my experience was based on that and went back last night positive that I would have a better time. 

I went back and still the same- not bad, not good just OK.. sort of like how something is just OK when you are eating at an airport. Leaving no real notion behind expect it being overpriced. 

I started out with the Kewpie Prawns. They were good don't get me wrong. They were lightly fried and then covered in a flavorful Kewpie Mayo sauce and then put on a bed of Japanese Watercress. The shrimps were tasty however at $18 the two prawn heads and 7 peices of cut up chunks of prawn was far from worth it. 

I then had the Spicy Red Chili Ramen and also the Dan Dan noodles. The ramen was just OK. It did have a latent spice to it and a nice soft boiled egg but the ramen itself was nothing special at all. No real depth of flavor on the broth. Noodles were just average, didn't taste freshly homemade. 

Dan Dan noodles were a real disappointment, not spicy at all (although they claimed it was) it was served with an egg yolk and a bowl of dry ground up chicken that you miss together. These really stunk. They lacked anything a good Dan Dan noodle has- szechuan peppercorn numbing, fresh noodles with a bite, etc. Before I could finish the bowl the noodles (served plain as you add in all the components) formed into a big stinky chunk that did not come apart. 

I am OK and expect to spend 15-18 dollars on a bowl of Ramen, it is NYC. However all their apps and drinks were very expensive.Dinner for four came over $200. So let's say $50 each which included one bowl of ramen with no extras, two beers and one shared prawn app. 

I went at 630 on a Wednesday night. I made sure to make reservations as I assumed it would be jammed packed. It was empty with plenty of tables- never a good sign. 

It's a real disappointment that after so much fanfare Ivan Ramen comes no where near it's hype.

There are SO many ramen places in NYC now skip this one.
Terrible service. Unbelievably rude. Do not go here! Food is good but service is not.

I really wanted to like this place. Having tried almost every ramen place in NY, I was hoping the hype would hold true and this would be one of the best bowls I've had. Unfortunately, this was not the case. I had the classic shoyu bowl and was shocked at how salty the broth was. I typically do not shy away from a lot of salt and consider my body to be somewhat cured at this point, considering how much salt I've consumed in my day. This bowl, however, tasted like dashi broth with bouillon cubes dissolved into it. Credit where it's due, the noodles themselves were quite good, as was the chasu.

My main qualm with my experience was not the food, but with the service. Paying top dollar for a bowl of noodles(same price as a base bowl at Ippudo, $15) one would expect exceptional service as well as decently sized portions. This was not the case. While extremely attentive while we ordered, our waitress seemed to completely forget about us after our order had been taken. This would be fine if the bowl had a lot of food in it, but it did not, and I was quickly left to go hungry after having finished my appetizer-sized entree. I wanted to order kaedama(extra noodles) but since we were completely forgotten by our server, I was unable to before my broth went cold. I would have ordered at least two more kaedama if had been given the opportunity. I decided to take my money elsewhere instead of dropping more undeserved cash on an establishment that was clearly unconcerned with it's customers' experience.

With so many Ramen options in NY, I will not return to this one. The food is nothing special and a much better value can be found elsewhere. Don't fall for the hype. Next time I want to pay top dollar for noodles I will return to Ippudo as I have so many times in the past.

Noodles lovers this is your place! Excellent quality of food with room for creativity. We had the chicken dan dan which was extremely spicy and the Tsukemen noodles. Before that we tried the pork and beets appetizer which was exceptional. A place worth visiting again, however it is quite pricey and can be crowded.

Cold shio ramen - nothing extraordinary and slightly better than instant ramen. Will satisfy your ramen craving, but you'll kinda wish you stood in line for ippudo

Bright interior, clean bathrooms, friendly and speedy service

I have to start with: this place falls victim to not living up to all its hype.

It was a drizzly Monday afternoon and I thought some warm noodle soup would cheer me right up. I was seated right away and the server came to fill my water immediately. I decided on the Classic Shoyu with extra enoki mushrooms. My first response when my noodles came was: that was fast. My second was: that's not a lot in the bowl...
I don't know if it was worth $2, but the mushrooms needed to be there or the bowl would've been really plain! I'm used to ramen being extremely flavorful, almost too much of a flavor explosion. Instead I was presented with an overly salty broth with noodles, a super thick piece of fat (with a little bit of pork on it), and a soft boiled egg. The rye noodles were interesting and I'm glad I've had them because now I know I'm a traditionalist who just wants normal ramen noodles.

What's weird is that all the food was cooked perfectly, the space was friendly and clean, and the service was great, but the style of food is so not my taste that I forget about all of that. I kept hearing that this place is good, but especially for the price, I am never coming here again.

been trying as many ramen places in the city as i can...and so far this place is my favorite. the spicy is perfect on a hot summer day or a cold winter one; its not overpoweringly spicy, but it will make your scalp sweat. service is quick and fast, and the location in LES makes it a great spot to stop before bar hopping or shopping.

bland ramen got the spicy choice, went there with a group of four and everyone agreed that this place is totally overrated and not worth the trek to les. actually i wouldnt go here even if i lived in the neighborhood. totto ramen much better. sorry excuse for a ramen place.

Ivan Ramen's appearance in NYC in 2014 has finally brought some competition to Ippudo's hold on the "fancy ramen" market here. If nothing else, you have to respect that a Long Islander founded a successful ramen shop in Tokyo. 

Ivan is the place I go to when my taste buds are craving the best flavors, but I don't have the energy to research the latest & greatest restaurants. It's also the place I go to when I have out-of-town friends to impress, but I don't want to deal with Ippudo's wait times. 

Great news for groups: Ivan Ramen now accepts reservations via OpenTable!

For appetizers/sides, make sure to order the Chinese Greens & Garlic (with garlic "love sauce"), for these reasons: 
- Ramen came from Chinese cuisine
- The flavor is addictive
- I mean, love sauce

I've witnessed people rave over other appetizers here (esp. the meatballs), but I'm not that into them.

My favorite ramen dishes at Ivan so far are the Triple Pork Triple Garlic Mazemen (less broth, not less tasty) and the chicken broth ramen that appears on the menu for limited periods of time. The latter is just the most velvety, umami-licious broth I have ever tried, and once it left the menu for summer I kept asking the staff when it would return. What I've heard so far is that they're thinking of bringing some alternative version of this ramen back for winter, with similar thick chicken broth. Whatever, I'll be there.

Chef Ivan is  from Long Island and has 2 ramen shops in Tokyo, BOTH  of these locations became some of the top ramen shops, this is unheard of for a foreigner to do. He then returned to NYC in 2012 to open up a ramen shop stateside. Once again his ramen has made it's way to the top of many best lists. 

 I love the decorations, and setup of the place, tons of cool art that blends Japanese and New York pop culture together. We requested the Tokyo Shio Ramen which is seasoned with sea salt and dashi. The broth is a very clean chicken broth topped with pork chashu, soft boiled egg and homemade rye noodles.
This was a pleasant surprise. Not only was the broth so different from the other bowls of ramen I've had before, but the rye noodles actually worked so perfectly and tasted amazing.
 It's weird to say, but the egg really means a lot to me in a ramen dish. 
voice over: If you can pull off a soft boiled egg it makes a world of difference to the rest of the ramen. Ivan gets it done perfectly right.
